AI.motivation: To challenge the dominant narrative that accelerating technological progress (Kurzweil's thesis) will naturally solve scientific discovery, by distinguishing between executional/infrastructural acceleration and the qualitatively different capacity of recognizing structural inadequacy in current frameworks.
AI.method: Mathematical interpretation of accelerating returns claim, analysis of ARC-AGI-3 benchmark results contrasting human vs. AI performance, and conceptual positioning of the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) framework.
AI.result: The gap between AI and human flexible reasoning remains very large (humans at ceiling, frontier AI below 1% on ARC-AGI-3), demonstrating that quantitative acceleration does not address the qualitative reasoning needed for genuine scientific discovery.
AI.conclusion: Kurzweil's theory explains quantitative capability acceleration, but QES addresses the missing capacity for structural reasoning in scientific discovery; the value of QES lies in preserving and transmitting human wisdom in the discovery process itself, independent of AGI arrival timelines.

title: Scaling Nonlinear Optimization: Many Problems One GPU
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, ieeeconf style, submission for RA-L
summary: Many robotics problems, including trajectory optimization, inverse kinematics, and contact-rich motion planning, reduce to nonlinear programs (NLPs). Mature NLP solvers such as IPOPT can solve these problems, offering hard constraint satisfaction, optimality guarantees, and favorable scaling with problem dimension. These solvers underpin gradient-based methods in robotics, yet remain CPU-bound and solve only one problem at a time, preventing their integration into GPU-batched learning pipelines. On the other hand, sampling-based approaches such as reinforcement learning, model predictive path integral, and imitation learning have become the core of modern robotics research due to their ability to leverage GPU-batched simulators. These simulators can generate orders of magnitude more dynamics rollouts per second than was previously possible. If a GPU-batched NLP solver existed, it would unlock similar speedups in the number of constrained, locally optimal solutions generated per second. This regime of solving many problems concurrently versus solving a single problem at a time is a key requirement for integrating NLP solvers in modern GPU-batched robotics frameworks. To this end, we introduce \texttt{jaxipm}, the first GPU-batched NLP solver, based on IPOPT, and implemented in JAX. We accomplish this by redesigning IPOPT's algorithm to eliminate control flow with \textit{heterogeneous iteration fusion}, and by minimizing GPU idle time with \textit{iteration level batching}. We evaluate \texttt{jaxipm} on a variety of quadrotor nonlinear model predictive control benchmarks, including reference tracking in the presence of obstacles, multi-quadrotor navigation without collision, and navigation in a cluttered environment. We demonstrate up to a $32.85\times$ increase in throughput over IPOPT. Our complete open-source codebase is available at https://github.com/johnviljoen/jaxipm.

AI.tldr: jaxipm is the first GPU-batched NLP solver implemented in JAX, redesigning IPOPT's algorithm with heterogeneous iteration fusion and iteration level batching to enable concurrent solving of nonlinear programs. It achieves up to 32.85× throughput improvement over IPOPT on quadrotor model predictive control benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing NLP solvers like IPOPT are CPU-bound and solve only one problem at a time, preventing integration into modern GPU-batched robotics learning pipelines (RL, MPPI, imitation learning) that leverage massive parallelism from GPU simulators.
AI.method: Redesigns IPOPT's algorithm in JAX by (1) heterogeneous iteration fusion to eliminate control flow, and (2) iteration level batching to minimize GPU idle time, enabling batched concurrent NLP solving.
AI.result: Up to 32.85× throughput increase over IPOPT on quadrotor nonlinear MPC benchmarks including obstacle-aware reference tracking, multi-quadrotor collision-free navigation, and cluttered environment navigation.
AI.conclusion: GPU-batched NLP solving unlocks orders-of-magnitude speedups in generating constrained locally optimal solutions, enabling integration of NLP solvers into modern GPU-batched robotics frameworks.

title: Narration-of-Thought: Inference-Time Scaffolding for Defeasible Ethical Reasoning in Large Language Models
comment: 24 pages, 8 figures, 16 tables. To appear at ACL 2026 (submitted via ARR)
summary: Standard chain-of-thought on moral dilemmas exhibits two failure modes: stakeholder collapse (the trace names at most one party with a stake in the outcome) and uncertainty suppression (no explicit unknowns or hedges before committing to an action). We introduce narration-of-thought (NoT), a system prompt that structures chain-of-thought into five sections: protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, then commitment. NoT adds no training, parameters, or fine-tuning. On 100 DailyDilemmas scenarios across four generators from three vendors, NoT cuts stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1% and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to 1-24% on every model. A matched-budget verbose-CoT control rules out token spend as the active ingredient; NoT retains Cliff's delta advantages of +0.79 to +0.90 on stakeholder count and +0.65 to +0.93 on uncertainty score for three of four generators, and a section ablation attributes each shift to its specific sub-instruction. Textual-gradient descent initialised at NoT improves the scaffold further; a cross-family training judge (different vendor from the generator) dominates an in-family one on every measured axis. Extended to a five-round multi-stakeholder debate protocol, the scaffold converts a 6% standoff into 95% full consensus on a calibration set and 100% combined convergence on a DailyDilemmas replication. The resulting traces externalise the stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainty grounding each commitment, providing an auditable substrate for dependable agentic deployment.

AI.tldr: Narration-of-Thought (NoT) is a structured system prompt that organizes chain-of-thought reasoning on moral dilemmas into five sections (protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, commitment), eliminating stakeholder collapse (from 31% to <1%) and uncertainty suppression (from 72% to 1-24%) across four LLM generators without training or fine-tuning. A text-gradient optimized variant and multi-round debate protocol further improve performance, producing auditable traces for dependable AI deployment.
AI.motivation: Standard chain-of-thought reasoning on moral dilemmas suffers from two critical failures: stakeholder collapse (naming at most one affected party) and uncertainty suppression (no explicit hedging before action commitment), undermining trustworthiness in agentic deployment.
AI.method: Introduces Narration-of-Thought (NoT), a structured system prompt forcing chain-of-thought into five sections: protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, then commitment. Evaluated on 100 DailyDilemmas scenarios across four LLM generators (from three vendors). Control experiments used matched-budget verbose-CoT and section ablation. Further optimization via textual-gradient descent and extension to a five-round multi-stakeholder debate protocol.
AI.result: NoT cuts stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1% and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to 1-24% on every model. Cliff's delta advantages of +0.79 to +0.90 on stakeholder count and +0.65 to +0.93 on uncertainty score for 3/4 generators. Textual-gradient descent improved the scaffold further. Multi-stakeholder debate converted 6% standoff to 95% full consensus (calibration) and 100% convergence (DailyDilemmas replication).
AI.conclusion: NoT provides a zero-training, zero-fine-tuning intervention that reliably externalizes stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainty in moral reasoning traces, creating an auditable substrate for dependable agentic deployment of LLMs.

title: MPC-Injection: Biasing Off-Policy Locomotion RL Toward Controller-Induced Behavior Basins
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for locomotion frequently converges to locally optimal but undeployable behaviors, such as vibrating limbs or scooting on the torso, that maximize return without producing a usable gait. We present MPC-Injection, a low-overhead method that steers RL toward a designer-preferred gait by inserting transitions into the replay buffer from a model predictive controller solving the same Markov decision process. Unlike reward shaping, MPC-Injection does not require redesigning the task reward, and unlike adversarial imitation learning, it adds no discriminator, no kinematic retargeting, and no auxiliary objective. Instead, the controller's preferred behavior is transferred to the policy purely through the replay state distribution. On a 2D walker in simulation and with sim-to-real evaluation on a Go2 quadruped, we show that MPC-Injection drives the policy into the controller's behavior basin using a one to two-term task reward, producing gaits qualitatively comparable to those of reward shaping with twenty-one tuned terms and of adversarial motion priors without their discriminator and retargeting overhead. We further analyze how the injected transitions bias actor-critic updates toward controller-visited states, allowing the policy to learn behaviors that pure RL may fail to reach under simple reward functions.

AI.tldr: MPC-Injection steers RL toward designer-preferred gaits by inserting model predictive controller transitions into the replay buffer, avoiding reward shaping complexity and adversarial imitation learning overhead.
AI.motivation: RL for locomotion often converges to locally optimal but undeployable behaviors (e.g., vibrating limbs, scooting on torso) that maximize return without producing usable gaits.
AI.method: MPC-Injection inserts transitions from a model predictive controller solving the same MDP into the RL replay buffer, biasing the replay state distribution toward controller-preferred behaviors without reward redesign or auxiliary objectives.
AI.result: On a 2D walker (simulation) and Go2 quadruped (sim-to-real), MPC-Injection produces gaits qualitatively comparable to reward shaping with 21 tuned terms and adversarial motion priors, using only a one-to-two-term task reward.
AI.conclusion: Injected transitions bias actor-critic updates toward controller-visited states, enabling the policy to learn behaviors that pure RL fails to reach under simple reward functions.

title: Geometry-Aware MCTS for Extremal Problems in Combinatorial Geometry
summary: We study certain extremal problems in combinatorial geometry that ask about configurations of points in an $n \times n$ grid that satisfy strict, global geometric constraints. Classical exact solvers suffer from combinatorial explosion for these types of problems, and standard reinforcement learning and transformer-based models struggle with the sparse reward "validity cliff" and quadratic token-consumption limits. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework. Our approach strictly enforces geometric constraints through incremental updates to the feasible action space. For constraints about collections of collinear points, like those that occur in the classic No-Three-in-Line problem (Max-N3IL), this mechanism reduces the constraint checking complexity from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$. To improve search efficiency, we exploit geometric symmetries in two ways: canonical pruning during node expansion to reduce the branching factor, and symmetric batch transitions to accelerate the discovery of promising configurations. We perform extensive experiments and establish new best-known computational results on five out of six of the problems that we considered. Notably, for Max-N3IL we find configurations of size roughly $1.8 n$ for grids of size $82 \le n \le 119$. For the Smallest Complete Set problem, we find configurations of size roughly $0.95 n$, providing new upper bounds within the tested grids. This work establishes Geometry-Aware MCTS as a highly adaptable framework for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework to solve combinatorial geometry problems on n×n grids, achieving new best-known results on five out of six problems, including configurations of ~1.8n points for Max-N3IL (n=82–119) and ~0.95n for the Smallest Complete Set problem.
AI.motivation: Classical exact solvers suffer from combinatorial explosion, while RL and transformer models struggle with sparse reward "validity cliffs" and quadratic token limits when solving extremal combinatorial geometry problems with strict global constraints.
AI.method: A Geometry-Aware MCTS framework that (1) strictly enforces geometric constraints via incremental feasible action space updates, reducing constraint checking complexity from O(n³) to O(n²) for collinearity constraints; (2) exploits geometric symmetries through canonical pruning to reduce branching factor and symmetric batch transitions to accelerate search.
AI.result: Established new best-known computational results on five of six problems. For Max-N3IL, found configurations of ~1.8n points for grids 82 ≤ n ≤ 119. For Smallest Complete Set, found configurations of ~0.95n, providing new upper bounds.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-Aware MCTS is a highly adaptable framework for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry.

title: Exploring the Intrinsic Geometry of Diffusion Models with Constrained Inverse Kinematics
summary: Recent studies suggest that diffusion models can recover geometric structure in the data manifolds they are trained on, yet the supporting evidence has so far come mostly from natural-image data, where the underlying geometry itself is unknown. We study this question in a setting where the geometry is analytically tractable: constrained inverse kinematics (IK). Each task-space constraint defines a configuration-space manifold with known intrinsic dimension, giving direct ground truth for evaluating the geometry learned by the model. For each of the 6-DoF UR5 and 7-DoF Franka, we train a single conditional diffusion model across seven constraint families, spanning solution manifolds from discrete IK branches to self-motion manifolds. Our empirical results reveal that the intrinsic dimension recovered from the model's score function matches the analytical degrees of freedom of the corresponding constraint manifold across both robots. Moreover, linear interpolation in the latent space leads to generated solutions that remain close to the appropriate constraint manifold, indicating that the learned representation further captures geometric structure of the constraint family beyond intrinsic dimension alone. Constrained IK therefore offers a controlled setting for studying the intrinsic geometry learned by diffusion models.

AI.tldr: Diffusion models trained on constrained inverse kinematics (IK) problems learn the intrinsic geometry of solution manifolds, recovering their true dimensionality and geometric structure across multiple constraint families for two robot arms.
AI.motivation: Prior evidence that diffusion models recover geometric structure in data manifolds has been limited to natural-image data where ground-truth geometry is unknown. The authors aim to study this question in a setting where geometry is analytically tractable: constrained inverse kinematics.
AI.method: Train a single conditional diffusion model across seven constraint families for two robot arms (UR5 and Franka). Evaluate the learned geometry by comparing the intrinsic dimension recovered from the model's score function against known analytical degrees of freedom of each constraint manifold. Also analyze linear interpolation in latent space.
AI.result: The intrinsic dimension recovered from the score function matches the analytical degrees of freedom of the corresponding constraint manifold for both robots. Linear interpolation in latent space yields solutions that stay close to the appropriate constraint manifold, showing the model captures geometric structure beyond intrinsic dimension.
AI.conclusion: Constrained IK provides a controlled setting for studying the intrinsic geometry learned by diffusion models, confirming they can recover both dimensionality and geometric structure of data manifolds.

title: When Agents Meet Electric Bus Fleet Operations: Pricing Behavior, Trade-offs, and Policy Implications in an Aggregator Framework
summary: Agentic systems are changing how complex operational tasks are coordinated, introducing a new paradigm for connecting heterogeneous data sources and automating processes. Electric bus fleets provide a relevant test case. Their operation requires continuous coordination between service reliability, battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) opportunities. This paper proposes an agentic aggregator framework that streamlines this decision environment by coupling an optimization-based electric bus scheduling model with supervisory agents for disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. The optimization core enforces physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges, while the agentic layer interprets changing operating conditions, triggers real-time re-optimization when needed, and defines how flexibility value is allocated between the aggregator and the public transport operator (PTO). A realistic depot case study evaluates day-ahead and real-time operations under profit-based and operation-based coordination modes, considering service delays, route-energy deviations, electricity price shocks, and combined disturbances. The results show that agentic aggregation can support adaptive fleet-grid coordination by maintaining feasible schedules, activating re-optimization selectively, and improving the use of charging and V2G flexibility. However, they also reveal a critical trade-off: the same agentic capability that reduces operational complexity can extract value from the PTO when configured around profit-oriented pricing. These findings suggest that agentic aggregators can become useful for managing electric bus V2G operations, but their deployment in public-fleet contexts requires transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting, and explicit value-sharing rules.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an agentic aggregator framework for electric bus fleet operations, combining optimization-based scheduling with supervisory agents for real-time disturbance detection and tariff adaptation. Results show improved adaptive fleet-grid coordination but reveal a critical trade-off where profit-oriented agentic configurations can extract value from public transport operators, necessitating transparent coordination and value-sharing rules.
AI.motivation: Electric bus fleet operation requires continuous coordination across multiple complex dimensions (service reliability, battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, and V2G opportunities), motivating a framework that streamlines this decision environment through agentic aggregation.
AI.method: The proposed agentic aggregator framework couples an optimization-based electric bus scheduling model (enforcing physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges) with supervisory agents for disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. The agentic layer interprets changing operating conditions, triggers real-time re-optimization, and defines flexibility value allocation between the aggregator and the public transport operator (PTO).
AI.result: Agentic aggregation supports adaptive fleet-grid coordination by maintaining feasible schedules, activating re-optimization selectively, and improving charging/V2G flexibility utilization. However, a critical trade-off emerges: profit-oriented configuration enables the agentic system to extract value from the PTO.
AI.conclusion: Agentic aggregators can be useful for managing electric bus V2G operations, but deployment in public-fleet contexts requires transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting, and explicit value-sharing rules to prevent value extraction from PTOs.

title: CoStream: Composing Simple Behaviors for Generalizable Complex Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon, contact-rich complex manipulation tasks, such as seating a GPU into a PCIe slot, demand both millimeter high precision and out-of-the-box generalization to new tasks. Existing paradigms struggle to satisfy both: classical pipelines use brittle, task-specific interfaces to achieve high-precision control but require costly pipeline redesigns to adapt to new tasks, whereas monolithic end-to-end policies provide better generalization but lack high precision on complex, out-of-distribution tasks unless retrained with new data. Both paradigms share an implicit assumption: once a manipulation capability is acquired, it must be deployed as a rigid pipeline or monolithic whole, rather than being freely decomposed and recomposed. In this paper, we show that complex manipulation capabilities can emerge naturally from the composition of simple, independent behaviors. Rather than deploying a monolithic policy or a rigid pipeline, we propose \ourshort, a framework orchestrating foundation models and diverse sensing modalities into multiple composable core behaviors: a semantic behavior extracting spatial constraints via foundation models; a predictive behavior forecasting trajectories by tracking keypoints in imagined videos; and a reactive behavior providing high-frequency tactile and force corrections. On a shared $SE(3)$ interface, these outputs compose by right-multiplication into a single pose command at each control step, executed by a compliant controller. We demonstrate \ourshort on 8 real-world tasks spanning everyday manipulation and precision assembly, with the strongest gains in contact-rich assembly and object transfer, and show robust recovery from manual perturbations during execution. {Website:} https://costream-simple.github.io

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CoStream, a framework that composes simple, independent behaviors (semantic, predictive, reactive) via a shared SE(3) interface to achieve both high precision and generalization in long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating strong results on 8 real-world tasks including GPU seating.
AI.motivation: Existing manipulation paradigms (classical pipelines vs. end-to-end policies) cannot simultaneously satisfy high precision and task generalization, as they assume manipulation capabilities must be deployed as rigid pipelines or monolithic wholes rather than composable components.
AI.method: CoStream orchestrates foundation models and diverse sensing modalities into three composable core behaviors: (1) semantic behavior extracting spatial constraints via foundation models; (2) predictive behavior forecasting trajectories by tracking keypoints in imagined videos; (3) reactive behavior providing high-frequency tactile and force corrections. These outputs compose via right-multiplication on a shared SE(3) interface into a single pose command at each control step, executed by a compliant controller.
AI.result: Demonstrated on 8 real-world tasks spanning everyday manipulation and precision assembly, with strongest gains in contact-rich assembly and object transfer, and robust recovery from manual perturbations during execution.
AI.conclusion: Complex manipulation capabilities can emerge naturally from the composition of simple, independent behaviors, challenging the implicit assumption that manipulation capabilities must be deployed as rigid pipelines or monolithic wholes.

title: Unbiased Canonical Set-Valued Oracles Via Lattice Theory
summary: A non-agentic "oracle" AI that estimates probabilities of future events faces a self-reference problem: once its answer is learned and acted upon, it can change the very probability it was asked to report. One response, advocated for the Scientist AI programme, is to ask only counterfactual questions, evaluated as if the answer had no influence. We observe that such answers tend to become irrelevant the moment they are learned, precisely because their premise is then false. We therefore explore a self-referential alternative in which the oracle reports not a single probability but a credal set that is simultaneously unbiased and self-consistent with the consequences of being learned. The naive self-consistency requirement is satisfied by too many sets (including the useless answer $[0,1]$), so the problem is to single out a canonical, nontrivial member. We do so with the Knaster--Tarski fixed-point theorem on the complete lattice of closed credal sets, taking the least fixed point of a suitably defined isotone operator; a variant instead reports the least fixed point that contains every self-consistent point estimate. We prove existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness, show that the construction collapses to the classical point answer for non-performative questions, and that for a binary event the canonical answer is, under a natural hull-factoring assumption, an interval. The development is purely lattice-theoretic and extends unchanged from a binary event $B$ to an arbitrary random variable $X$, with $P(B\mid A,C)$ replaced by the conditional law $\mathcal{L}(X\mid A,C)$. We close with open questions, including whether the interval characterization itself survives that generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a self-referential oracle AI that, instead of reporting a single probability for a future event (which becomes invalid once learned and acted upon), reports a credal set (a set of probabilities) that is self-consistent with the consequences of being learned. The authors use the Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem on the complete lattice of closed credal sets to single out a canonical, nontrivial fixed point, proving existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness, and showing it collapses to classical point estimates for non-performative questions.
AI.motivation: Standard oracle AIs face a self-reference problem: once their probability estimate is learned and acted upon, it changes the very probability they were asked to report. The Scientist AI programme's counterfactual approach yields answers that become irrelevant once learned. Therefore, a self-referential alternative is needed that accounts for the performative effects of its own disclosure.
AI.method: The paper models the oracle as reporting a credal set (closed convex set of probability distributions) rather than a single probability. It defines an isotone operator on the complete lattice of closed credal sets and applies the Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem to obtain the least fixed point as the canonical answer. A variant finds the least fixed point containing every self-consistent point estimate. The framework is lattice-theoretic and generalizes from binary events to arbitrary random variables via conditional laws.
AI.result: Proves existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness of the canonical fixed-point credal set. Shows the construction collapses to the classical point answer for non-performative questions. For binary events, under a natural hull-factoring assumption, the canonical answer is an interval. The development extends to arbitrary random variables with conditional laws replacing conditional probabilities.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous fixed-point framework for self-referential probabilistic oracles, producing nontrivial, self-consistent credal sets. Open questions remain, including whether the interval characterization for binary events generalizes to arbitrary random variables.

title: A System for Fast, Resilient, and Adaptable Loco-Manipulation Behaviors on Humanoid Robots
comment: PhD dissertation, University of West Florida, Department of Intelligent Systems and Robotics, June 2026. 331 pages
summary:
Humanoid robots could take on physically demanding, hazardous, and repetitive work in spaces built for humans. However, a useful robot for these spaces must coordinate locomotion, whole body motion, perception, contact, and operator supervision. This thesis presents a robot-local, runtime-editable behavior authoring and runtime system.
  Our system strives to be maximally observable, predictable, and directable following Coactive Design principles developed during the DARPA Robotics Challenge. Our operator interface remains continuously synchronized to the robot for runtime authoring, monitoring, and repair. Our behavior architecture uniquely combines object-centric Affordance Templates, organization and logic inspired by Behavior Trees, and runtime-editable perception through a behavior scene and primitive scene actions. Action primitives build on a whole-body controller that supports moving the arms while walking, and use a concurrent action layering algorithm for speed.
  The behavior library developed during this work covers more than twenty real-robot task variants, including push and pull doors with knob, push-bar, and lever-handle mechanisms, multi-step exploration sequences, obstacle clearing, and reactive table-to-table manipulation tasks. This behavior system has been deployed on many humanoid robots, such as Boston Dynamics' DRC Atlas, NASA's Valkyrie, IHMC and Boardwalk Robotics' Nadia, Unitree's H1-2, and IHMC's Alex.
  We evaluate our system across capability, speed, reliability, and speed of behavior creation, adaptation, extension, and combination. Our experiments demonstrate that we can adapt, extend, and combine existing behaviors to create novel loco-manipulation behaviors in minutes or hours. Videos: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLJK5CTyotYqsfgfnXb-09YNFeBose6uEY.

AI.tldr: This thesis presents a robot-local, runtime-editable behavior authoring and runtime system for humanoid robots that combines Affordance Templates, Behavior Trees, and runtime-editable perception to enable observable, predictable, and directable robot behaviors across diverse manipulation tasks, deployed on multiple humanoid platforms.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots need to operate in human-built spaces performing physically demanding, hazardous, and repetitive work, but existing systems lack sufficient observability, predictability, and directability for practical operator supervision and runtime adaptation.
AI.method: The system combines object-centric Affordance Templates, Behavior Tree-inspired organization/logic, runtime-editable perception via a behavior scene and primitive scene actions, a whole-body controller supporting arm movement during walking, and a concurrent action layering algorithm for speed, following Coactive Design principles for operator-robot collaboration.
AI.result: The behavior library covers 20+ real-robot task variants (push/pull doors with various mechanisms, exploration, obstacle clearing, table-to-table manipulation). Deployed on Atlas, Valkyrie, Nadia, H1-2, and Alex. Experiments demonstrate adaptation, extension, and combination of existing behaviors to create novel loco-manipulation behaviors in minutes or hours.
AI.conclusion: The system enables rapid creation and modification of complex loco-manipulation behaviors on humanoid robots, achieving practical runtime editability and operator-directed control across multiple platforms.

title: Estimating Uncertainty in Classifier Performance with Applications to Large Language Models and Nested Data
summary: Researchers increasingly use text classification--supervised models or large language models--to measure constructs from natural language, providing metrics such as recall and precision as evidence of their validity. Yet, though these metrics are point estimates subject to sampling variation, measures of uncertainty are inconsistently reported alongside them. Further, when they are reported, they are often estimated with methods that are not appropriate when relevant labelled datasets are small or performance is high. To increase and improve confidence interval reporting in the field, this paper evaluates confidence interval methods for performance metrics under conditions typical of social science text classification: small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals. Across simulations, default methods such as the Wald interval and the basic percentile bootstrap are the least accurate, with coverage sometimes far below the nominal 95% level. Accuracy is improved with the use of Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap (which is particularly relevant to the calculation of F1). When texts are nested within individuals, we demonstrate that adjustment for both effective N and the appropriate degrees of freedom is necessary for producing accurate analytic intervals. Among bootstrap intervals, the hierarchical bootstrap is more accurate than the cluster bootstrap when individuals produce a moderate number of texts but overly conservative when individuals produce only a few. By providing guidance to the field on appropriate interval estimation, we aim to improve the transparency of machine learning applications, and to encourage greater attention to the validation sample size at the design stage.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates confidence interval methods for text classification performance metrics under typical social science conditions (small samples, rare constructs, nested texts), finding that default methods like Wald intervals and basic percentile bootstrap are inaccurate, while Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap perform better, with hierarchical bootstrap preferred for nested data.
AI.motivation: Researchers using text classification (supervised models or LLMs) to measure constructs from natural language inconsistently report uncertainty measures for performance metrics like recall and precision, and when reported, these use methods inappropriate for small labeled datasets or high performance levels.
AI.method: Simulations evaluating confidence interval methods for performance metrics under conditions typical of social science text classification: small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals.
AI.result: Default methods (Wald interval, basic percentile bootstrap) are least accurate with coverage far below nominal 95%; Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap (for F1) improve accuracy; for nested texts, adjustment for effective N and appropriate degrees of freedom is necessary; hierarchical bootstrap outperforms cluster bootstrap for moderate text counts.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides guidance on appropriate interval estimation to improve transparency of machine learning applications and encourages greater attention to validation sample size at the design stage.

title: Play2Perfect: What Matters in Dexterous Play Pretraining for Precise Assembly?
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://play2perfect.github.io
summary: Multi-fingered robots promise the speed and dexterity of human hands, yet challenging problems such as precise assembly have remained out of reach. These tasks are contact-rich, making data collection for imitation learning difficult, and sparse-reward, making direct exploration with reinforcement learning (RL) intractable. Consequently, prior work has made progress by structuring the problem with specialized grippers, tool attachments, and environment fixtures. In this work, we argue that before a robot can perfect precise assembly, it must first learn to play. We further ask the question: what factors in the process of learning to play matter for precise assembly? We propose Play2Perfect, an RL framework for task-agnostic pretraining through play on diverse objects and goals, which is then perfected on precise assembly. The goal of play is to acquire reusable manipulation priors, such as grasping, in-hand reorientation and pose reaching. Finetuning then adapts this general prior to assembly, focusing exploration on the final contact-rich, high-precision interactions needed for success. We systematically study key design choices in play pretraining, including object diversity, training objective, trajectory diversity, and goal precision. We show that our prior is 33x more sample-efficient than RL training from scratch, even when provided with dense, multi-stage rewards. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, achieving 60% success on tight insertions with only 0.5 mm contact clearance, and over 50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing.

AI.tldr: Play2Perfect is an RL framework that pretrains on diverse play tasks to acquire reusable manipulation priors, then fine-tunes for precise assembly, achieving 33x sample efficiency and 60% success on tight insertions with 0.5mm clearance.
AI.motivation: Multi-fingered robots struggle with precise assembly due to contact-rich, sparse-reward environments that make imitation learning and RL difficult. Prior work relied on specialized grippers and fixtures; this work aims for a more general solution.
AI.method: A two-stage RL framework: (1) task-agnostic pretraining through play on diverse objects and goals to learn reusable manipulation priors (grasping, in-hand reorientation, pose reaching); (2) finetuning on precise assembly tasks to focus exploration on contact-rich, high-precision interactions.
AI.result: 33x more sample-efficient than RL from scratch; zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with 60% success on tight insertions (0.5mm clearance), >50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing.
AI.conclusion: Learning to play first is an effective pretraining strategy for precise assembly, and key design choices (object diversity, trajectory diversity, goal precision) significantly impact downstream performance.

title: Data-driven Machine Learning Cannot Reach Symbolic-level Logical Reasoning -- The Limit of the Scaling Law
summary: Sphere neural networks have achieved symbolic level syllogistic reasoning without training data, raising the question of where the limit of the scaling law for logical reasoning lies, i.e., whether data-driven machine learning systems can achieve the same level by increasing training data and training time. We show two methodological limitations that prevent supervised deep learning from reaching the symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning: (1) training data can not distinguish all 24 types of valid syllogistic reasoning; (2) end-to-end mapping from premises to conclusion introduces contradictory training targets between neural components for pattern recognition and logical reasoning. Beside theoretical analysis, we experimentally illustrate that Euler Net cannot achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning. We further challenge the most recent ChatGPTs (GPT-5-nano and GPT-5) to determine the satisfiability of syllogistic statements in four surface forms (patterns): words, double words, simple symbols, and long random symbols, showing that surface forms affect the reasoning performance and that ChatGPT GPT-5 may reach 100% accuracy but still provide incorrect explanations. As empirical training processes are stopped after achieving 100% accuracy, we conclude that supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigour of symbolic logical reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that supervised deep learning systems cannot achieve the rigorous syllogistic reasoning of symbolic-level neural networks, due to two fundamental limitations: indistinguishable training data across valid syllogism types and contradictory training targets from end-to-end mapping. Experiments with Euler Net and ChatGPT (GPT-5-nano, GPT-5) show that even 100% accuracy is misleading, as models still produce incorrect explanations and are affected by surface form variations.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether data-driven supervised machine learning systems can achieve the same level of symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning as sphere neural networks (which do so without training data), thereby probing the limits of scaling laws for logical reasoning.
AI.method: The authors (1) theoretically identify two methodological limitations of supervised deep learning for syllogistic reasoning, (2) experimentally evaluate Euler Net's syllogistic reasoning capabilities, and (3) test ChatGPT variants (GPT-5-nano and GPT-5) on syllogistic satisfiability across four surface forms (words, double words, simple symbols, long random symbols).
AI.result: Euler Net fails to achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning. ChatGPT's performance is affected by surface form variations; GPT-5 can reach 100% accuracy but still provides incorrect explanations, indicating a lack of genuine logical rigor despite high accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigor of symbolic logical reasoning, as empirical training processes stop once 100% accuracy is achieved without resolving the underlying methodological limitations.

title: WatchAct: A Benchmark for Behavior-Grounded Robot Manipulation
summary: A robot working alongside people must reason about what they have done, in what order, and with what intent. Video carries the spatial layouts, object histories, and gestures that language leaves underspecified, yet today's manipulation benchmarks pair an instruction with a single current image, offering no way to evaluate reasoning over observed human behavior. We introduce WatchAct, a benchmark for robot manipulation grounded in observed human behavior. Each instance pairs a real-world human-action video and a language instruction with an aligned simulator scene and an executable LIBERO task, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation. WatchAct comprises 3,000 long-horizon instances across 14 tasks in four capability domains drawn from the cognitive demands of watching another agent: parsing events (Event Grounding), recovering procedural structure (Procedural Reasoning), inferring unstated intent (Implicit Intent Inference), and tracking how the scene was changed (Episodic Reasoning). We further propose a disentangled evaluation protocol that separately measures (i)~video-to-plan reasoning by vision-language models, (ii)~policy execution under oracle plans, and (iii)~full task completion by integrated planner--policy pipelines. In both simulation and on a Franka Research 3 robot, current systems remain far from solving WatchAct. The best pipeline, Gemini-3.1-Pro with $π_{0.5}$, reaches only 16.3% Success Rate (SR) in simulation and 14.0% on the real robot. Gemini-3.1-Pro attains just 36.8% Plan SR (vs. 97.1% for humans), while $π_{0.5}$ reaches only 21.5% Task SR under oracle plans and drops to 10.6% on out-of-domain scenarios. Dataset and code are available at https://baiqi-li.github.io/watchact_page/.

AI.tldr: WatchAct is a benchmark for robot manipulation that tests reasoning over observed human behavior through 3,000 long-horizon instances across 14 tasks in four cognitive domains. Current systems perform poorly, with the best pipeline achieving only 16.3% simulation and 14.0% real-robot success rates.
AI.motivation: Existing manipulation benchmarks pair instructions with single static images, failing to evaluate a robot's ability to reason over observed human behavior (actions, sequences, intents) captured in video.
AI.method: WatchAct creates 3,000 instances by pairing real-world human-action videos with language instructions, aligned simulator scenes, and executable LIBERO tasks. It defines four capability domains (Event Grounding, Procedural Reasoning, Implicit Intent Inference, Episodic Reasoning) and a disentangled evaluation protocol measuring video-to-plan reasoning, policy execution under oracle plans, and full pipeline task completion.
AI.result: Best pipeline (Gemini-3.1-Pro + π₀.₅) achieves 16.3% Success Rate in simulation and 14.0% on real Franka Research 3 robot. Gemini-3.1-Pro attains 36.8% Plan SR vs. humans' 97.1%; π₀.₅ reaches 21.5% Task SR under oracle plans, dropping to 10.6% on out-of-domain scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Current vision-language models and policy networks are far from solving WatchAct, indicating substantial room for improvement in robot reasoning over observed human behavior.

title: MKG-RAG-Bench: Benchmarking Retrieval in Multimodal Knowledge Graph-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs has emerged as a promising approach for grounding large language models, yet existing benchmarks largely overlook the challenges of retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph RAG (MKG-RAG). In practice, retrieval is a critical bottleneck: multimodal knowledge is heterogeneous, difficult to align across modalities, and often poorly served by retrievers designed for unstructured corpora. To address this gap, we introduce MKG-RAG-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate retrieval in MKG-RAG. MKG-RAG-Bench is constructed from two multimodal knowledge graphs spanning general and medical domains, and includes carefully aligned question-answering datasets that support controlled evaluation of both retrieval and downstream generation. The benchmark is built using an LLM-based curation pipeline that filters low-utility knowledge, generates structurally grounded queries with exact supervision, and systematically covers diverse modality configurations. Through extensive experiments across representative retriever families and modality settings, we show that effective multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet crucial for end-to-end MKG-RAG performance, and that retrieval quality strongly determines generation outcomes. By isolating retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a principled foundation for diagnosing current limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

AI.tldr: MKG-RAG-Bench is a benchmark designed to evaluate retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems, showing that multimodal retrieval remains challenging and is critical for generation performance.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG benchmarks overlook retrieval challenges in multimodal knowledge graph settings where knowledge is heterogeneous, hard to align across modalities, and poorly served by conventional retrievers.
AI.method: The benchmark is constructed from two multimodal KGs (general and medical domains), uses an LLM-based curation pipeline to filter low-utility knowledge, generate structurally grounded queries with exact supervision, and systematically cover diverse modality configurations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across representative retriever families and modality settings show that effective multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet crucial for end-to-end MKG-RAG performance, and retrieval quality strongly determines generation outcomes.
AI.conclusion: By isolating retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a principled foundation for diagnosing limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

title: OSC2Runner: OpenSCENARIO 2.x Compliant High-Fidelity AV Simulation in CARLA
comment: Accepted at 26th IEEE International Conference on Software Quality, Reliability, and Security (QRS 2026)
summary: Scenario-Based Testing predominantly relies on the legacy ASAM OpenSCENARIO 1.x XML standard because existing continuous simulation frameworks lack native execution support for the recently matured v2.x Domain-Specific Language (DSL). Adapting legacy interpreters to evaluate v2.x logic introduces spatiotemporal drift, asynchronous event latencies, and artificial kinematic snapping. Addressing this execution gap, OSC2Runner introduces the first orchestration framework capable of natively mapping the OpenSCENARIO v2.x DSL to CARLA. The framework achieves this by formalizing scenario translation as a compilation pipeline through a multi-pass transpiler architecture. Bypassing static trajectory playback, the architecture synthesizes type-safe Abstract Syntax Trees directly into dynamic deterministic behavior trees (py_trees) natively mapped to CARLA's atomic APIs. Empirical validation in highly concurrent adversarial case studies demonstrates tick-by-tick determinism, exact spatial trigger evaluation, and 100.0 ms cross-actor blackboard synchronization. Kinematic analysis proves the strict adherence to continuous environmental boundaries. This architecture transitions Scenario-Based Testing from approximate behavioral interpretation to mathematically rigorous execution, establishing the deterministic backend required for co-simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and automated LLM-driven generation pipelines.

AI.tldr: OSC2Runner is the first native orchestration framework that maps OpenSCENARIO v2.x DSL to CARLA via a multi-pass transpiler, achieving deterministic behavior tree execution with exact spatial triggers and 100ms cross-actor synchronization.
AI.motivation: Existing Scenario-Based Testing frameworks rely on ASAM OpenSCENARIO 1.x XML due to lack of native v2.x DSL support; adapting legacy interpreters introduces spatiotemporal drift, asynchronous latencies, and kinematic snapping.
AI.method: The framework formalizes scenario translation as a multi-pass transpiler pipeline: it synthesizes type-safe ASTs from v2.x DSL and compiles them into dynamic deterministic behavior trees (py_trees) natively mapped to CARLA's atomic APIs, bypassing static trajectory playback.
AI.result: Empirical validation demonstrates tick-by-tick determinism, exact spatial trigger evaluation, 100.0 ms cross-actor blackboard synchronization, and strict adherence to continuous environmental boundaries in highly concurrent adversarial cases.
AI.conclusion: This architecture shifts Scenario-Based Testing from approximate interpretation to mathematically rigorous execution, providing the deterministic backend required for co-simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and LLM-driven generation pipelines.

title: auto-psych: Automating the science of mind using agent-driven theory discovery and experimentation
summary: AI-based scientific automation is increasingly possible by using agents to generate hypotheses, design experiments, and analyze data. Data collection is a major bottleneck in this pipeline, however. Psychology, and computational cognitive science in particular, is well-positioned to benefit from AI experimentation because theories are often represented as code and crowdsourcing platforms enable programmatic human data collection at scale. Here, we apply automated discovery techniques to the project of generating theories in computational cognitive science, with an agent-based system collecting human data independently through crowdsourced survey experiments. As a testbed, we use a classic case study from cognitive psychology: judging which sequences of coin flips seem subjectively more random. Our system, auto-psych, uses nested agent-based discovery loops to generate explanatory theories of human behavior. The inner loop conjectures, fits, and critiques probabilistic cognitive models; the outer loop designs experiments to test these models, launches them online, and analyzes the data. This system can quickly and reliably recover ground-truth theories from synthetic data via systematic experimentation, but the nested structure is critical to model performance. Further, in three independent sequences of human experiments, the system finds theories that fit the data better than theories generated from the scientific literature. This work thus demonstrates the feasibility of automated data collection and theory discovery in computational cognitive science.

AI.tldr: The paper presents auto-psych, an agent-based system that autonomously generates theories, designs and conducts crowdsourced experiments, and fits cognitive models to human data, demonstrating successful automated discovery in computational cognitive science using the case study of subjective randomness judgments of coin flips.
AI.motivation: Data collection is a major bottleneck in AI-based scientific automation. Psychology and computational cognitive science can benefit from AI experimentation because theories are often code-based and crowdsourcing enables scalable human data collection, motivating the development of an end-to-end automated discovery system.
AI.method: The auto-psych system employs nested agent-based discovery loops: an inner loop conjectures, fits, and critiques probabilistic cognitive models, while an outer loop designs experiments, launches them on crowdsourcing platforms, and analyzes the resulting human data. The system was tested on the classic cognitive psychology case study of perceived randomness in coin flip sequences.
AI.result: The system reliably recovered ground-truth theories from synthetic data, with the nested structure being critical for performance. In three independent sequences of human experiments, auto-psych found theories that fit the data better than existing theories from the scientific literature.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of automated data collection and theory discovery in computational cognitive science, showing that AI-driven agent systems can autonomously conduct end-to-end scientific discovery cycles including hypothesis generation, experiment design, human data collection, and model fitting.

title: IDEA: Insensitive to Dynamics Mismatch via Effect Alignment for Sim-to-Real Transfer in Multi-Agent Control
summary: Complex multi-agent control tasks remain challenging for traditional rule-based and model-based approaches, motivating the adoption of learning-based methods. However, learning-based methods often struggle with sim-to-real transfer because they rely on accurate dynamics modeling or system identification and learn policies in low-level control spaces that are highly sensitive to dynamics mismatch, making them costly and fragile in complex environments. To address this issue, we propose a sim-to-real method for multi-agent control, which is insensitive to dynamics mismatch via effect alignment. Our method combines random environmental structure with discrete semantic actions through closed-loop control, elevating policy learning to a semantic abstraction level. Additionally, we develop an action synchronization mechanism that mitigates inter-agent action timing mismatches, thereby enhancing the temporal consistency of the system. Experiments on four multi-agent navigation tasks demonstrate that our method substantially improves training efficiency over mainstream transfer methods and achieves higher success rates in real-world scenarios, thereby improving the robustness and deployment stability of multi-agent systems under dynamics mismatch.

AI.tldr: A sim-to-real method for multi-agent control that uses effect alignment via random environmental structures and discrete semantic actions, along with action synchronization, to achieve dynamics-mismatch-insensitive policy learning and robust real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Learning-based multi-agent control methods struggle with sim-to-real transfer due to sensitivity to dynamics mismatch from accurate dynamics modeling or system identification requirements, making them costly and fragile in complex environments.
AI.method: The method combines random environmental structure with discrete semantic actions via closed-loop control to elevate policy learning to a semantic abstraction level, and develops an action synchronization mechanism to mitigate inter-agent action timing mismatches.
AI.result: Experiments on four multi-agent navigation tasks show substantially improved training efficiency over mainstream transfer methods and higher success rates in real-world scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed effect-alignment-based sim-to-real method improves robustness and deployment stability of multi-agent systems under dynamics mismatch.

title: Clinical Harness for Governable Medical AI Skill Ecosystems
summary: Medical AI remains organized around isolated models, whereas clinical care requires accountable capabilities that persist across time. We propose clinical AI skills and the Clinical Harness: a runtime governance architecture for registering, orchestrating, guarding and monitoring AI-enabled clinical capabilities. Using osteoporosis as an exemplar, we show how knowledge-driven, data-driven and physics-enhanced skills can support lifecycle care under runtime governance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a runtime governance architecture called the Clinical Harness for managing AI-powered clinical capabilities as persistent, accountable "skills," demonstrated through osteoporosis care.
AI.motivation: Medical AI currently consists of isolated models that lack persistence and accountability, failing to meet the needs of continuous clinical care.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Clinical Harness, a runtime governance architecture that registers, orchestrates, guards, and monitors AI-enabled clinical skills. They use osteoporosis as an exemplar to demonstrate knowledge-driven, data-driven, and physics-enhanced AI skills supporting lifecycle care.
AI.result: The proposed architecture enables the integration of diverse AI skill types (knowledge-driven, data-driven, physics-enhanced) under a unified runtime governance framework for lifecycle care in osteoporosis.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from isolated AI models to persistent, governed clinical skills is necessary for accountable AI in clinical care; the Clinical Harness provides a viable architecture for this transition.

title: Inference-Time Robot Behavior Steering through Physically-Aware Reconfiguration of Task-Structure
summary: A central challenge in deploying learned robot policies is inference-time behavior steering: redirecting a policy at test time to satisfy user preferences not anticipated during training, without retraining. Existing methods fail in two modes: end-to-end methods require fine-tuning or expert-level guidance, while neuro-symbolic methods rely on predefined symbols whose edits can result in logically reasonable but physically infeasible plans. To address this challenge, we propose ReStruct, which builds upon a neural automaton policy that decomposes a visuomotor policy into a high-level state-machine skeleton capturing task structure and a low-level continuous controller represented as a residual policy. Specifically, ReStruct adopts the automaton to represent the preference and incorporates it into the skeleton through a synchronous product, thereby reconfiguring the task structure. With the controller kept frozen, the action priors provided by the skeleton are updated accordingly to enable physically-aware control under a modified task structure. Extensive experiments from simulation and real-world show that ReStruct steers a wide range of preferences, from object-centric specifications to temporal-logic constraints, and after steering surpasses existing methods, exceeding VLA models in both task success and preference-following by up to 25%.

AI.tldr: ReStruct is a method for inference-time behavior steering of learned robot policies that uses a neural automaton to decompose policies into a high-level state-machine skeleton and low-level residual controller, then reconfigures the skeleton via synchronous product to incorporate user preferences without retraining, outperforming existing methods including VLAs by up to 25%.
AI.motivation: The key challenge is enabling inference-time behavior steering of learned robot policies to satisfy user preferences not anticipated during training, without retraining. Existing end-to-end methods require fine-tuning or expert guidance, while neuro-symbolic approaches rely on predefined symbols whose edits can yield logically reasonable but physically infeasible plans.
AI.method: ReStruct builds upon a neural automaton policy that decomposes a visuomotor policy into a high-level state-machine skeleton (task structure) and a low-level continuous controller (residual policy). It adopts the automaton to represent the preference and incorporates it into the skeleton through a synchronous product, reconfiguring the task structure. The controller remains frozen, and action priors from the skeleton are updated for physically-aware control under the modified task structure.
AI.result: Extensive simulation and real-world experiments show ReStruct steers a wide range of preferences (from object-centric specifications to temporal-logic constraints) and surpasses existing methods including VLA models in both task success and preference-following by up to 25%.
AI.conclusion: ReStruct effectively addresses inference-time behavior steering by combining the strengths of neuro-symbolic structure with frozen low-level control, achieving both logical consistency and physical feasibility without retraining.

title: Humans Disengage, Reasoning Models Persist: Separating Difficulty Registration from Deliberation Allocation
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) take longer on harder problems, just as humans do. This surface similarity hides an opposite pattern within items. When an LRM gets a problem wrong, it spends more tokens than when it gets the same problem right; humans do the reverse, spending less time on the trials they get wrong. We separate two levels of deliberation: how response time tracks difficulty across items (registration), and, with item identity held fixed, whether an agent spends more on its own failures or successes (allocation). On a public matched human-LRM corpus, humans and all five thinking LRMs reproduce the known cross-item alignment (registration) but diverge within items (allocation): every LRM shows a large wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47-3.13 on H-ARC) while humans show the opposite sign. The comparison stays inside each agent's own scale; we never put seconds and tokens on one axis. The dissociation holds under item fixed effects, replicates across datasets, and is absent in a non-thinking baseline. We read the human pattern as engagement versus abandonment: people stay on items they expect to solve and give up on the rest. We read the LRM pattern as length driven by uncertainty: chains grow when the model is unsure, which is exactly when it tends to fail. Both policies produce the same cross-item correlation with difficulty, so they look aligned on the measure prior work has used; the divergence shows up only once item identity is fixed. Under resource-rational metareasoning, the split is between two stopping policies that share a difficulty signal but implement opposite control; trace length captures the signal and misses the control.

AI.tldr: Large reasoning models (LRMs) and humans both spend more time on harder problems (cross-item alignment), but diverge within the same problem: LRMs spend more tokens on failures than successes, while humans do the opposite. This reveals that cross-item difficulty correlations mask opposite within-item allocation policies—LRMs increase computation when uncertain (and fail), while humans disengage when they expect to fail.
AI.motivation: Prior work assumes that longer response times (humans) or token counts (LRMs) simply reflect problem difficulty, treating the correlation between time and difficulty as evidence of alignment. This paper unpacks this correlation into two levels—registration (cross-item difficulty tracking) and allocation (within-item success vs. failure)—to reveal a hidden divergence between human and LRM deliberation policies.
AI.method: Using a public matched human-LRM corpus (H-ARC and other datasets), the authors compare response time/tokens across items (registration) and within items (allocation) for humans and five thinking LRMs. They employ item fixed effects to isolate within-item variation and compute Cohen's d for the wrong-vs-right token effect, contrasting with human time allocation. A non-thinking baseline is included as a control.
AI.result: All agents show the same cross-item registration (harder items take longer/more tokens). However, within items, every LRM exhibits a large wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47–3.13 on H-ARC), spending more tokens on failures, while humans show the opposite sign. The pattern replicates across datasets and is absent in non-thinking baselines.
AI.conclusion: Humans and LRMs implement opposite within-item stopping policies despite sharing a difficulty signal: humans disengage when expecting failure (abandonment), while LRMs increase computation when uncertain, which is when failure is likely. Under resource-rational metareasoning, trace length captures the difficulty signal but misses the control policy, meaning cross-item alignment alone is insufficient to claim human-like deliberation.

title: Bridging Handheld and Teleoperated Supervision for Contact-Rich Manipulation via State-Gated Experts
summary: Handheld data collection systems, such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI), enable scalable data collection across diverse environments but only capture observed actions rather than the desired actions executed by a robot controller. In contrast, teleoperation captures desired actions directly, but is prohibitively time-consuming to collect. We revisit this trade-off through the lens of action validity across task phases. We observe that handheld trajectories provide valid supervision in tolerant, free-space phases, but lack dynamic feasibility in contact-sensitive phases, where tracking observed trajectories at high stiffness produces large, unsafe contact forces. We study the interaction between these two supervision types for contact-rich manipulation and find that training policies that combine handheld data with a small number of targeted teleoperated demonstrations provide an efficient hybrid strategy. Specifically, rather than teleoperating the entire task, we only collect partial teleoperated demonstrations for task segments where base handheld policies fail. However, naively mixing handheld and teleoperated phase-specific data yields worse performance than training on handheld data alone. To address this mismatch between observed and desired supervision, we propose Bi-modal Routing for Imitation Data via Gated Experts (BRIDGE), a mixture of diffusion policy experts that routes between specialist task phase heads conditioned on the current robot state. Notably, our approach enables task-phase specific use of desired actions during contact sensitive segments and improves success rates over handheld-only baselines by up to 36.7% across three contact-rich manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: BRIDGE is a hybrid imitation learning framework that combines efficient handheld data collection (for free-space phases) with minimal teleoperated demonstrations (for contact-sensitive phases) using a gated mixture of diffusion policy experts, improving success rates by up to 36.7% over handheld-only baselines in contact-rich manipulation.
AI.motivation: Handheld data collection (e.g., UMI) is scalable but captures observed actions lacking dynamic feasibility in contact-sensitive phases, while teleoperation captures desired actions but is prohibitively time-consuming. The paper revisits this trade-off and seeks an efficient hybrid strategy that leverages the strengths of both.
AI.method: The authors propose BRIDGE (Bi-modal Routing for Imitation Data via Gated Experts), a mixture of diffusion policy experts that routes between specialist task-phase heads conditioned on the current robot state. Handheld data is used for tolerant free-space phases, while a small number of targeted partial teleoperated demonstrations are collected only for contact-sensitive segments where the base handheld policy fails.
AI.result: Naively mixing handheld and teleoperated data yields worse performance than handheld-only data. BRIDGE addresses this mismatch and improves success rates by up to 36.7% across three contact-rich manipulation tasks compared to handheld-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: Task-phase-specific use of desired actions during contact-sensitive segments is effective. The hybrid strategy combining scalable handheld data with minimal targeted teleoperation via a gated expert architecture provides an efficient paradigm for contact-rich manipulation.

title: NeuraDock Visual Cognitive Load Agent Tutorial: A Quality-Gated Open-Source EEG Workflow for Alpha Dynamics and Real-Time Applications
summary: This tutorial paper provides a step-by-step, reproducible walkthrough of NeuraDock Agent, an open-source EEG agent focused on Alpha dynamics and visual cognitive-load analysis. The goal is practical: a reader should be able to install the agent, run EEG preprocessing and quality control, generate Alpha dynamics figures, perform within-subject Rest/Task visual cognitive-load comparison, run the public mini-dataset analyses and compare them with the reference validation summary, start an online dashboard, call the real-time API from an external application, and use the LLM interpretation layer to explain quality risks. Existing EEG toolkits provide excellent offline analysis, but assembling a real-time, quality-gated cognitive-load pipeline often requires manually bridging acquisition, custom QC, Alpha feature extraction, and a web API; this tutorial closes that offline-to-online gap. The tutorial uses a quality-gated workflow: downstream Alpha and workload metrics are computed only after preprocessing and QC gating rather than directly from raw EEG. In the included mini-dataset validation, the agent processed 18 recordings, generated 10 within-subject comparisons, observed task-related posterior Alpha suppression in 7 of 10 contrasts, estimated initial evidence of within-subject repeatability, and benchmarked local online API latency. The tutorial is intended for researchers, developers, and applied teams who want a transparent path from EEG files to real-time visual cognitive-load prototypes.

AI.tldr: NeuraDock Agent is an open-source EEG agent providing a step-by-step tutorial for real-time, quality-gated visual cognitive-load analysis using Alpha dynamics, with validation on 18 recordings showing posterior Alpha suppression in 7 of 10 within-subject comparisons.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG toolkits offer excellent offline analysis but require manually bridging acquisition, custom QC, Alpha feature extraction, and web API for real-time, quality-gated cognitive-load pipelines; this tutorial closes the offline-to-online gap.
AI.method: Quality-gated workflow: EEG preprocessing and QC gating precede downstream Alpha and workload metric computation; includes installation instructions, preprocessing, Alpha dynamics figure generation, within-subject Rest/Task comparison, mini-dataset validation, online dashboard, real-time API, and LLM-based interpretation layer.
AI.result: Processed 18 recordings, generated 10 within-subject comparisons, observed task-related posterior Alpha suppression in 7 of 10 contrasts, estimated within-subject repeatability, and benchmarked local online API latency.
AI.conclusion: NeuraDock Agent provides a transparent, reproducible path from raw EEG files to real-time visual cognitive-load prototypes, suitable for researchers, developers, and applied teams.

title: A Closed-Form 4-DoF Inter-Robot Pose Estimator using Bearing-only Measurements
summary: Bearing-odometry-based cooperative localization has attracted increasing research interest due to its minimal infrastructure requirements, low communication bandwidth and broad applicability in complex environments. However, existing 6-DoF approaches still face challenges in rapidly obtaining accurate and reliable inter-robot pose estimation, as the system is prone to observability degeneracy under specific motion patterns. To address these issues, we first propose a closed-form 4-DoF inter-robot pose estimator, which relaxes nonlinear constraints for rotations estimation and employs error projection for translations estimation. We then conduct a theoretical analysis of the system's observability, identifying degeneracy under two typical motion patterns: collinear and shape-preserving formations. The analysis further shows that the proposed 4-DoF system requires less stringent motion excitation for observability, enabling reliable estimation under a broader range of cooperative maneuvers. Furthermore, an observability test module is introduced to autonomously determine the optimal estimation instant, eliminating reliance on a predefined fixed-length sliding window. Extensive simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves higher estimation accuracy with significantly low computational cost, and the observability test module ensures estimation reliability while minimizing the data collection interval.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a 4-DoF inter-robot pose estimator for bearing-odometry cooperative localization, addressing observability degeneracy issues in 6-DoF systems. It introduces a closed-form estimator with error projection, theoretical observability analysis identifying degeneracy under collinear/shape-preserving formations, and an observability test module for adaptive estimation timing. The method achieves higher accuracy with lower computational cost and reliable estimation under broader motion conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing 6-DoF bearing-odometry cooperative localization approaches struggle to quickly obtain accurate and reliable inter-robot pose estimation due to observability degeneracy under specific motion patterns.
AI.method: Proposes a closed-form 4-DoF inter-robot pose estimator that relaxes nonlinear constraints for rotation estimation and uses error projection for translation estimation. Conducts theoretical observability analysis identifying degeneracy under collinear and shape-preserving formations. Introduces an observability test module to autonomously determine optimal estimation instant without a fixed-length sliding window.
AI.result: Higher estimation accuracy with significantly lower computational cost; observability test module ensures estimation reliability while minimizing data collection interval; the 4-DoF system requires less stringent motion excitation for observability, enabling reliable estimation under broader cooperative maneuvers.
AI.conclusion: The proposed 4-DoF approach effectively overcomes observability degeneracy limitations of 6-DoF methods, achieving both accuracy and efficiency in bearing-odometry-based cooperative localization.

title: Boundary-Aware Context Grounding for A Low-Channel EEG Agent
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) can make scientific software easier to use. However, a general model does not automatically know which measurements a particular sensor can support, which algorithms are implemented in the current software, or which conclusions are justified by a computed result. These distinctions are especially important for low-channel electroencephalography (EEG), where sparse spatial coverage and variable signal quality make plausible but unsupported interpretations easy to produce. We present NeuraDock Agent, an open-source architecture that separates a deterministic local EEG engine from a hardware-aware language layer. The numerical engine parses recordings, performs quality control, executes reviewed spectral workflows, and writes machine-readable artifacts. The LLM receives only a compact, allowlisted summary and a versioned context pack. The context describes the seven-channel hardware, reviewed workflows, result fields, implementation boundaries, scientific limits, and reference cases. Raw EEG and dense per-sample arrays remain local
  We evaluate the system at three levels. First, 12 recordings produced identical structured results over ten numerical repetitions, and a complete Rest/Task run produced identical result, report, and figure hashes over three repetitions. Second, request-capture and failure-injection experiments confirmed the tested data boundary and preservation of local artifacts under HTTP, malformed-output, and connection failures. Third, a boundary-awareness benchmark tested 36 ordinary and adversarial questions under four context ablations and two LLMs, yielding 288 outputs.These results support hardware- and implementation-aware grounding as a practical mechanism for calibrating what an EEG agent accepts, qualifies, or refuses; they do not establish clinical validity or a validated absolute cognitive-load index.

AI.tldr: NeuraDock Agent is an open-source architecture that separates a deterministic local EEG engine from a hardware-aware LLM layer to prevent unsupported scientific interpretations in low-channel EEG analysis.
AI.motivation: LLMs lack inherent knowledge of specific sensor capabilities, software implementations, and scientifically justified conclusions for EEG data, especially low-channel EEG where sparse spatial coverage and variable signal quality make unsupported interpretations easy to produce.
AI.method: The system separates a deterministic local EEG engine (parsing, quality control, spectral workflows, machine-readable artifacts) from an LLM that only receives a compact allowlisted summary and versioned context pack describing hardware, workflows, result fields, boundaries, and reference cases. Raw EEG data remains local.
AI.result: (1) 12 recordings produced identical structured results over 10 numerical repetitions; Rest/Task run produced identical hashes over 3 repetitions. (2) Boundary and failure-injection tests confirmed data boundary preservation under HTTP and connection failures. (3) A 288-output boundary-awareness benchmark (36 questions × 4 context ablations × 2 LLMs) tested ordinary and adversarial questions.
AI.conclusion: Hardware- and implementation-aware grounding is a practical mechanism for calibrating what an EEG agent accepts, qualifies, or refuses; clinical validity or a validated absolute cognitive-load index is not established.

title: Hardware Design for Table Tennis Robot Capable of Beating Professional Players
comment: 8 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables. The supplementary video can be downloaded from "Ancillary files"
summary: This paper focuses on the hardware specifications required for a table tennis robot to beat professional players. After analyzing the motions of elite players, we defined target specifications for the workspace, payload, external-force resistance, physical performance, serve capability, and end-effector accuracy. Based on these specifications, we developed "Ace", a custom 8-DoF robot. The mechanical structure was improved through topology optimization to minimize mass while preserving stiffness. Motor and gearbox selection was optimized using an inverse-dynamics torque model. Low-order per-joint dynamics models with delay compensation were identified and integrated into simulation to enable the use of an RL control policy. Experiments demonstrated repeated full-stroke swings with a cycle time of 0.8 s and a peak racket-center velocity of 22 m/s. The robot successfully defeated multiple professional players.
