summary: Robots deployed in the real world rarely operate under a single fixed dynamics model: wind changes, payloads vary, batteries drain, contacts shift, and hardware wears. Yet most learning-based controllers are trained once and deployed as if learning were complete. This prevents the robot from using deployment experience to further improve task performance. In this work, we propose a continual learning framework that uses real-world experience to improve robot policies under hidden and recurring dynamics. Our method learns a condition-aware dynamics model from real state-action trajectories by combining an analytical physics prior with a neural residual for unmodeled effects. A recurrent encoder infers the current hidden condition from recent interaction, and this estimate conditions both the residual model and the policy. Policy learning is performed via differentiable simulation using diverse learned dynamics sampled from the latent model. At deployment, these sampled conditions are replaced by conditions inferred online from recent real interaction, allowing the policy to recover recurring dynamics by recognition rather than residual re-fitting. Through extensive simulation studies and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that the framework improves policy performance under diverse unobserved disturbances. On real quadrotor trajectory tracking under changing wind, the policy recovers from recurring disturbances in roughly 1s, about 5x faster than online residual re-fitting. It also reduces large-disturbance hover and tracking errors by 65.7% and 53.3% over the state-of-the-art online adaptation approaches

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a continual learning framework that uses real-world experience to improve robot policies under hidden and recurring dynamics, combining physics priors with neural residuals and recurrent encoding for condition awareness, achieving significant improvements in quadrotor trajectory tracking under changing wind conditions.
AI.motivation: Robots deployed in real-world environments face changing dynamics (wind, payload, battery drain, contact shifts, hardware wear), yet most learning-based controllers are trained once and deployed without leveraging deployment experience to improve task performance.
AI.method: The framework learns a condition-aware dynamics model by combining an analytical physics prior with a neural residual for unmodeled effects. A recurrent encoder infers the current hidden condition from recent interaction, conditioning both the residual model and policy. Policy learning uses differentiable simulation with diverse learned dynamics, and deployment replaces sampled conditions with online-inferred conditions for recognition-based recovery.
AI.result: On real quadrotor trajectory tracking under changing wind, the policy recovers from recurring disturbances in ~1s (5x faster than online residual re-fitting), and reduces large-disturbance hover and tracking errors by 65.7% and 53.3% over state-of-the-art online adaptation approaches.
AI.conclusion: The continual learning framework enables robots to improve policies under diverse unobserved disturbances by recognizing recurring dynamics rather than residual re-fitting, significantly outperforming existing online adaptation methods.

title: Generative Retrieval via Diffusion Transformer with Metric-Ordered Sequence Training and Hybrid-Policy Preference Optimization
summary: Embedding-based retrieval ranks items by their similarity to a query in a shared vector space and usually aims to return the highest-scoring items. In many production settings this is not what is wanted: given a seed set that expresses a fine-grained pattern, one needs more items that both satisfy a target attribute and stay within that pattern. We formalize this as pattern-preserving attribute retrieval. The two goals pull against each other: averaging the seeds preserves the pattern but stays in a low-attribute region, while global attribute retrieval drifts to unrelated patterns. We approach the task with continuous generative retrieval, where a model reads a sequence of item embeddings and generates query embeddings for nearest-neighbor search. We propose MO-DiT+HPPO, a staged framework with raw-sequence pretraining, multi-domain metric-ordered continuation pretraining, tail-centroid fine-tuning, and HPPO. Metric-ordered training turns sparse online retrieval labels into in-pattern trajectories ordered from low to high predicted attribute density, teaching one model the metric-improvement direction across domains. HPPO aligns the generated query distribution with the true online objective by labeling a hybrid candidate pool with the online intersection metric and applying reference-anchored preference optimization. A Pareto pair filter keeps only winner pairs that do not lower same-pattern purity, raising the attribute metric without sacrificing the pattern. Across four attribute domains under item- and pattern-holdout protocols, metric-ordered DiT improves the intersection metric over a pretrained generative retriever, and HPPO improves it further, with significant gains on seven of eight domain-split cells and a marginal tie on the hardest split. Metric-predictor validation, order ablations, CPT/SFT comparisons, and a candidate-policy ablation show where the gains come from.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MO-DiT+HPPO, a staged generative retrieval framework for pattern-preserving attribute retrieval. It uses raw-sequence pretraining, multi-domain metric-ordered continuation pretraining, tail-centroid fine-tuning, and HPPO (hybrid preference optimization) to retrieve items that satisfy a target attribute while staying within a fine-grained pattern defined by a seed set. Experiments across four attribute domains show significant improvements in intersection metrics over baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard embedding-based retrieval aims for highest-scoring items, but in production settings the goal is often different: given a seed set expressing a fine-grained pattern, one needs items that satisfy a target attribute while staying within that pattern. These two objectives conflict—averaging seeds preserves the pattern but yields low attribute scores, while global attribute retrieval drifts to unrelated patterns. The paper formalizes this tension as pattern-preserving attribute retrieval.
AI.method: MO-DiT+HPPO is a staged framework with four components: (1) raw-sequence pretraining, (2) multi-domain metric-ordered continuation pretraining (ordering sparse retrieval labels into low-to-high predicted attribute density trajectories to teach metric-improvement direction across domains), (3) tail-centroid fine-tuning, and (4) HPPO (Hybrid Preference Policy Optimization)—labeling a hybrid candidate pool with the online intersection metric and applying reference-anchored preference optimization with a Pareto pair filter that removes pairs reducing same-pattern purity.
AI.result: Across four attribute domains under item- and pattern-holdout protocols, metric-ordered DiT improves the intersection metric over a pretrained generative retriever, and HPPO improves it further. Significant gains are achieved on seven of eight domain-split cells, with a marginal tie on the hardest split. Ablations (metric-predictor validation, order ablations, CPT/SFT comparisons, candidate-policy ablation) confirm the source of improvements.
AI.conclusion: The proposed staged generative retrieval framework effectively addresses the pattern-preserving attribute retrieval problem, achieving strong improvements by teaching metric-improvement direction across domains via metric-ordered training and aligning query distributions with the true online objective via HPPO with Pareto pair filtering.

title: RouterVLA: Turning Smoke Tests into Supervision for Heterogeneous VLA Selection
summary: We study whether pre-deployment evaluation rollouts can be reused to supervise policy selection. Robot teams routinely smoke test candidate vision-language-action (VLA) policies, then compress those trials into a global winner. RouterVLA evaluates this idea with outcome-disjoint cross-fitting: recorded probes build a profile for each frozen expert, and a separate trial scores the selected expert without entering its profile. Across 34,752 LIBERO-Plus rollout records, a transparent probe-success rule raises held-out success from 0.4686 to 0.6149, a +14.64pp gain. Under the scalar-only profiles studied here, learned scorers are statistically indistinguishable from this rule, showing that commissioning carries the routing value while extra scalar scorer capacity does not create it. Reusing the scored trial inflates the measured gain by $1.87\times$, so credible ledger routing needs outcome separation; model scaling improves individual policies, while commissioning-aware routing improves the system built from them.

AI.tldr: RouterVLA shows that pre-deployment evaluation rollouts can be reused for policy selection via outcome-disjoint cross-fitting, achieving a +14.64pp gain in success rate, and demonstrates that transparent probe-success rules are as effective as learned scorers while model scaling and commissioning-aware routing provide complementary benefits.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether pre-deployment evaluation rollouts (which are routinely collected to smoke test VLA policies) can be reused to supervise policy selection, avoiding the need for separate routing data.
AI.method: Proposes outcome-disjoint cross-fitting (RouterVLA): recorded probes build a profile for each frozen expert, and a separate trial scores the selected expert without entering its profile. Uses 34,752 LIBERO-Plus rollout records with transparent probe-success rules and learned scalar-only scorers.
AI.result: A transparent probe-success rule raises held-out success from 0.4686 to 0.6149 (+14.64pp). Learned scalar-only scorers are statistically indistinguishable from this rule. Reusing the scored trial inflates the measured gain by 1.87×.
AI.conclusion: Commissioning (evaluation rollouts) carries the routing value; extra scalar scorer capacity does not create it. Credible ledger routing requires outcome separation (no trial leakage). Model scaling and commissioning-aware routing provide complementary improvements.

title: Learning to Recover Task Experts from a Multi-Task Merged Model
summary: Multi-task model merging aims to consolidate several task-specific experts into a unified model, yet static merging consistently suffers from parameter interference. While dynamic merging models aim to bridge this gap, many works rely on the costly storage and loading of redundant expert components at inference. In this work, from the perspective of task expert, we view parameter interference as parameter perturbation introduced to each expert during merging process. We show that such parameter perturbations can be modeled as affine transformation, which can be approximated as additive offsets. Motivated by these, we propose Recover Task eXpert (ReTeX), a framework that predicts those offsets, in order to undo parameter interference and recover task-expert performance from a single merged checkpoint. To recover the appropriate expert when task identity is unknown, we introduce a router-free task identifier based on SVD subspace signatures computed offline before inference. At inference, the identifier selects the task whose subspace yields the smallest projection residual for a given input. As a result, ReTeX recovers over 95% of individual-expert performance in both vision and NLP domains, while significantly improving generalization to unseen tasks. Crucially, we also show that the parameter offset prediction leads to emergent adaptive interpolation of expert knowledge for out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. ReTeX adaptively interpolates seen expert knowledge to handle unseen tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/BAIKLAB/ReTeX

AI.tldr: ReTeX recovers task-expert performance from a single merged model by predicting and removing parameter interference (modeled as affine offsets) during merging, using a router-free SVD subspace identifier to handle unknown tasks, achieving >95% individual expert performance recovery and OOD generalization.
AI.motivation: Multi-task model merging suffers from parameter interference between task-specific experts when merged statically. Dynamic merging reduces interference but requires costly storage and loading of redundant expert components at inference, motivating the need for an efficient method that recovers expert performance from a single checkpoint without storing multiple experts.
AI.method: ReTeX models parameter interference as affine transformations approximated as additive offsets. It predicts these offsets to undo interference and recover task-expert performance. For unknown task identity, it uses a router-free task identifier based on SVD subspace signatures computed offline; at inference, it selects the task whose subspace yields the smallest projection residual for a given input.
AI.result: ReTeX recovers over 95% of individual-expert performance in both vision and NLP domains, significantly improves generalization to unseen tasks, and shows emergent adaptive interpolation of expert knowledge for out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks.
AI.conclusion: Parameter interference in merging can be effectively undone by predicting and removing additive offsets from a single merged checkpoint, enabling strong performance recovery and generalization without storing redundant expert components at inference.

title: World Action Models Enable Continual Imitation Learning with Recurrent Generative Replays
summary: Going beyond predicting robot actions, World Action Models (WAMs) can also generate future visual observations. We build on this generative capability to propose Recurrent Generative Replay (REGEN), a continual imitation learning framework that synthesizes pseudo-replay trajectories, enabling a robot policy to rehearse previously learned tasks without storing their original human demonstrations. During continual adaptation, REGEN recursively queries the WAM to synthesize pseudo-replay trajectories conditioned only on prior task instructions and current-task observations. Experiments in both simulation and real-world manipulation settings show that REGEN reduces catastrophic forgetting by up to $50\%$ relative to sequential fine-tuning, while approaching the performance of privileged experience replay methods that require access to real replay data. Finally, we analyze the factors limiting generated replay, identifying long-horizon visual degradation and action-observation inconsistency as the primary bottlenecks. Our results establish WAMs as a promising foundation for continual robot learning without stored demonstrations.

AI.tldr: REGEN uses World Action Models to generate pseudo-replay trajectories for continual imitation learning, reducing catastrophic forgetting by up to 50% without storing original human demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Enable continual robot learning without storing original human demonstrations, mitigating catastrophic forgetting in imitation learning settings.
AI.method: REGEN recursively queries a World Action Model to synthesize pseudo-replay trajectories conditioned on prior task instructions and current-task observations, avoiding the need for stored replay buffers.
AI.result: Reduces catastrophic forgetting by up to 50% compared to sequential fine-tuning, approaching the performance of privileged experience replay, with long-horizon visual degradation and action-observation inconsistency identified as primary bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: World Action Models are a promising foundation for continual robot learning without stored demonstrations.

title: Diagnosing Task Insensitivity in Language Agents
summary: Large language models can serve as capable long-horizon agents, but their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains weak. We identify a key source of this failure as task insensitivity: when faced with similar but distinct tasks, models might apply patterns learned during training and fail to solve the task at hand. We show that models often continue with actions aligned with the original task even when the instruction is semantically corrupted and cannot be directly answered. We further find that, when we replace the task description in a trained prompt with another similar but distinct task, the model may still output the same action. This behavior is accompanied by a consistent training-time attention drift away from task tokens and toward local observations, suggesting an optimization bias toward shortcuts. To mitigate this problem, we propose Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization, a lightweight contrastive regularizer that explicitly encourages action dependence on the task instruction. Extensive evaluations show that our intervention improves task sensitivity and OOD generalization while preserving more stable attention to task tokens.

AI.tldr: LLMs as long-horizon agents suffer from out-of-distribution generalization failure due to task insensitivity—they ignore task instructions and rely on shortcuts. The authors propose Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization, a contrastive regularizer that improves task sensitivity and OOD generalization.
AI.motivation: To identify and address the root cause of poor OOD generalization in LLM-based long-horizon agents, which is attributed to task insensitivity—models ignoring task instructions and defaulting to learned patterns.
AI.method: Proposes Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization, a lightweight contrastive regularizer that explicitly encourages action dependence on task instructions. The method is motivated by empirical findings showing attention drift away from task tokens toward local observations during training.
AI.result: The proposed method improves task sensitivity and OOD generalization while preserving more stable attention to task tokens, as demonstrated through extensive evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Task insensitivity is a key failure mode for OOD generalization in LLM agents, and the proposed contrastive regularization effectively mitigates this issue by enforcing stronger reliance on task instructions.

title: Scalable Behavior Cloning with Open Data, Training, and Evaluation
summary: We introduce ABC, a fully open-source stack for manipulation with behavior cloning. At its core is ABC-130K: the largest open-source teleoperation dataset to date, featuring 3,500 hours of data spanning over 130K episodes across 195 diverse tasks. Furthermore, we open-source our accessible hardware setup, training infrastructure, and simulation pipeline. We also release 400 hours of sim-teleop data and provide a co-training recipe that produces correlated simulation and real-world evaluation, offering a reliable proxy for ablating model-design and training decisions before costly real-world evaluation. We explore various training recipes and compare common architectural choices for Diffusion Transformers (DiT) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, grounding our findings in real-world evaluations. The resulting policies successfully execute dexterous tasks such as box folding and extracting credit cards from wallets. By providing a reproducible toolkit, we aim to place researchers on an equal footing, establishing the necessary foundation to learn the ABCs of Behavior Cloning together as a community.

AI.tldr: ABC introduces the largest open-source teleoperation dataset (ABC-130K: 3,500 hours, 130K+ episodes, 195 tasks) along with fully open-source hardware, training infrastructure, simulation pipeline, and co-training recipes for behavior cloning, enabling reproducible real-world dexterous manipulation research.
AI.motivation: To democratize behavior cloning research by providing a fully open-source, reproducible stack (hardware, data, training, simulation) that addresses the lack of large-scale, accessible resources for manipulation policy learning.
AI.method: 1) Collected ABC-130K dataset (3,500 hours, 130K+ episodes, 195 tasks) via teleoperation. 2) Open-sourced hardware setup, training infrastructure, and simulation pipeline. 3) Released 400 hours of sim-teleop data with a co-training recipe for correlated sim-to-real evaluation. 4) Benchmarked Diffusion Transformers (DiT) vs. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models under various training recipes.
AI.result: Policies trained on ABC achieve dexterous tasks like box folding and credit card extraction from wallets. The co-training recipe provides correlated sim and real-world evaluation as a reliable proxy before costly real-world tests.
AI.conclusion: ABC provides a reproducible toolkit that places researchers on equal footing, establishing foundational resources for the community to collectively advance behavior cloning for manipulation.

title: Where Do CoT Training Gains Land in LLM based Agents?
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is widely used in language-model agents, but prior work has shown that verbalized CoT is not always faithful and may instead reflect post-hoc reasoning, which means the model already knows the answer before reasoning. We therefore ask what CoT training is actually improving: is the model getting better at changing its action through generated reasoning, or is it getting better at predicting the action directly from the prompt? We study this question by comparing \emph{prompt actions} (predicting action without CoT) with CoT actions (predicting action with CoT). Across checkpoints, prompt-action quality improves substantially. While interacting with the environment, the relative advantage of CoT actions over prompt actions remains similar, showing that CoT training does not widen the advantage of CoT reasoning, and it helps to improve the quality of prompt actions. We further find that later checkpoints are less likely to revise the action in response to CoT, suggesting greater reliance on the prompt. Motivated by these patterns, we selectively mask action-token supervision on a fraction of training examples. This intervention improves out-of-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether CoT training improves reasoning-based action generation or direct prompt-to-action mapping. Findings show CoT training primarily improves prompt-action quality rather than reasoning advantage, and later checkpoints rely more on prompts. Selective masking of action-token supervision improves generalization.
AI.motivation: To understand what CoT training actually improves in language-model agents—whether it enhances reasoning-based action generation or simply improves direct prompt-to-action prediction—given prior evidence that verbalized CoT can be post-hoc and unfaithful.
AI.method: Compare prompt actions (predicting action without CoT) with CoT actions (predicting action with CoT) across checkpoints; analyze the relative advantage of CoT over prompt actions; examine action revision likelihood in response to CoT; propose selective masking of action-token supervision on a fraction of training examples.
AI.result: Prompt-action quality improves substantially across checkpoints; the relative advantage of CoT over prompt actions remains similar throughout training; later checkpoints are less likely to revise actions in response to CoT; selective masking of action-token supervision improves out-of-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: CoT training primarily enhances the model's ability to predict actions directly from prompts rather than improving reasoning-based decision-making. Selective masking of action-token supervision can mitigate over-reliance on prompt-action mapping and improve generalization.

title: Look-Before-Move: Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention in Dynamic 3D Story Worlds
summary: As embodied AI and world models increasingly operate in dynamic 3D environments, visual perception must move beyond passively interpreting given observations toward actively deciding what to observe. We study this problem through camera planning in dynamic 3D story worlds, where the camera must not only generate smooth motion, but also decide what visual evidence should be acquired before it moves. We formulate this capability as Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention, where the camera acts as an embodied observer that determines what to observe, how to compose the observation, and how to shift attention over time under narrative intent and physical 3D constraints. To realize this capability, we propose Look-Before-Move, a camera planning framework that separates observation specification from motion execution. It first builds a Semantic Observation Contract to convert directorial intent into executable visual constraints, then performs Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search to find narrative-compliant and geometrically feasible viewpoints, and finally applies Semantic Trajectory Grounding to connect selected viewpoints into continuous, collision-aware, and temporally coherent camera motion. We further construct a dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark based on StoryBlender, covering 50 stories, 457 scenes, and 1585 shots with animated characters, semantic scene configurations, and executable 3D environments. Experiments show that our framework improves subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality over representative baselines, demonstrating the importance of organizing visual attention before generating camera motion.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Look-Before-Move, a camera planning framework for dynamic 3D story worlds that first decides what visual evidence to acquire before generating camera motion, using Semantic Observation Contracts, Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search, and Semantic Trajectory Grounding, demonstrating improved perception and intent consistency over baselines on a new StoryBlender benchmark.
AI.motivation: Embodied AI and world models need visual perception that actively decides what to observe in dynamic 3D environments, beyond passively interpreting given observations. Current camera planning lacks the ability to determine what visual evidence should be acquired before moving.
AI.method: The Look-Before-Move framework consists of three components: (1) Semantic Observation Contract — converts directorial intent into executable visual constraints; (2) Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search — finds narrative-compliant and geometrically feasible viewpoints; (3) Semantic Trajectory Grounding — connects viewpoints into collision-aware, temporally coherent camera motion. A dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark based on StoryBlender (50 stories, 457 scenes, 1585 shots) is constructed for evaluation.
AI.result: The framework improves subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality over representative baselines, demonstrating the importance of organizing visual attention before generating camera motion.
AI.conclusion: Organizing visual attention before motion generation is crucial for effective camera planning in dynamic 3D story worlds; the proposed framework successfully separates observation specification from motion execution.

title: Einstein World Models
summary: Does intelligence require the ability to reason about phenomena beyond direct experience? It is natural to suspect that some complex thought cannot be captured through language alone. However, of particular concern to this work, is whether visualising counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought. We ask whether LLMs can be trained to utilise such visualisation mechanisms, in a way that benefits their reasoning abilities. Motivated by this question, we propose Einstein World Models. EWMs are a blueprint for LLM-based reasoning systems that place visual-temporal rollouts inside the reasoning trace, allowing them to reason in ways that text alone may not support well. In an EWM, the LLM calls a world-module (not to be confused with a world model), to produce short rollouts of scenes under consideration. The returned rollout is treated not as the answer, but as an inspectable hypothesis that can support later reasoning. Einstein World Models extend the capability of LLMs for tool calling (such as web search or code execution), into the domain of visual thought experiments.

AI.tldr: Proposes Einstein World Models (EWMs), a framework that augments LLMs with a world-module capable of generating visual-temporal rollouts (counterfactual visualizations), which serve as inspectable hypotheses within the reasoning trace to improve reasoning beyond what text alone can support.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether visualizing counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought, and whether LLMs can be trained to utilize such visualizations to benefit their reasoning abilities.
AI.method: EWMs integrate an LLM with a world-module that produces short visual-temporal rollouts of scenes under consideration. These rollouts are treated as inspectable hypotheses (not final answers) within the reasoning trace, extending LLM tool-calling capabilities (e.g., web search, code execution) into the domain of visual thought experiments.
AI.result: The paper presents a blueprint/system design; specific experimental results are not detailed in the abstract, but the claim is that EWMs enable LLMs to reason in ways that text alone may not support well.
AI.conclusion: Visual-temporal rollouts can serve as a complementary mechanism to language for complex reasoning in LLMs, and EWMs provide a structured way to incorporate this capability via tool-calling paradigms.

title: Adaptive Utility driven Resource Orchestration for Resilient AI (AURORA-AI)
comment: Accepted at IEEE Research and Technologies for Society and Industry 2026 conference
summary: Modern AI systems are increasingly deployed under non-stationary computational, demographic, and operational conditions in which static resource allocation strategies degrade both predictive performance and human-centric properties such as fairness and explainability. This paper presents AURORA-AI, an Adaptive Utility-driven Resource Orchestration framework for Resilient AI that unifies Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman feedback control, Lyapunov-based stability monitoring, and a fairness-aware composite utility into a single closed-loop policy.The framework continuously redistributes computational budget across a population of heterogeneous AI models so that the global utility, defined jointly over predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability, remains maximised under disruption. The framework is evaluated in a stress-rich discrete-time simulation that concurrently injects demographic bias shocks, gradual concept drift, and abrupt black-swan disruptions, and is compared against five established controllers including Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, and a deep reinforcement-learning agent based on Proximal Policy Optimisation. AURORA-AI achieves immediate recovery from the black-swan event compared to eighty-eight time steps for the Static baseline and twenty-two for Proximal Policy Optimisation, lifts the alpha-quantile and the super-quantile by twenty-nine and twenty-five percent respectively, simultaneously reduces the mean and maximum demographic parity gap, and increases the fraction of Lyapunov-stable operating steps. These results indicate that fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory is a practical and theoretically motivated path toward resilient human-centric AI deployment.

AI.tldr: AURORA-AI is an adaptive resource orchestration framework leveraging Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman control, Lyapunov stability, and fairness-aware utility to dynamically allocate computational budgets across heterogeneous AI models under non-stationary conditions, achieving faster recovery from disruptions, improved fairness, and higher stability compared to five baselines.
AI.motivation: Modern AI systems face non-stationary computational, demographic, and operational conditions where static resource allocation degrades predictive performance and human-centric properties like fairness and explainability, necessitating adaptive orchestration.
AI.method: AURORA-AI unifies Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman feedback control, Lyapunov-based stability monitoring, and a fairness-aware composite utility (predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, interpretability) into a closed-loop policy that continuously redistributes computational budgets across heterogeneous AI models.
AI.result: Achieved immediate black-swan recovery vs. 88 steps (Static) and 22 steps (PPO); lifted alpha-quantile by 29% and super-quantile by 25%; reduced mean and max demographic parity gap; increased Lyapunov-stable operating steps.
AI.conclusion: Fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory provides a practical and theoretically motivated path toward resilient human-centric AI deployment.

title: Semantic Early-Stopping for Iterative LLM Agent Loops
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Open implementation, machine-checked theory, and reproducible harness: github.com/SahilShrivastava-Dev/semantic-halting-problem
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) loops, for example a Writer that drafts and a Critic that revises, are almost always terminated by a fixed iteration cap (max_iterations). This is a syntactic kill-switch: it is blind to whether the answer is still improving, so it over-spends tokens on easy inputs and truncates hard ones. We study semantic early-stopping: the loop halts when consecutive draft embeddings stop changing in meaning (cosine distance with a patience window) and the answer's measured quality stops improving. Our work makes three contributions. First, an honest theoretical footing: we prove deterministic termination and well-definedness and machine-check these claims, while treating the convergence of the distance sequence as an empirically tested conjecture rather than a (previously over-claimed) Banach contraction. Second, a judge-efficient evaluation protocol: we generate each question's full trajectory once, replay every stopping policy over the identical drafts, and cache every LLM-judge call, yielding a strictly paired efficiency-versus-quality comparison at low cost; we further separate operational tokens (charged to a policy) from evaluation tokens (a measurement instrument). Third, an empirical study on multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering (HotpotQA). On the 60-question test split, a judge-free semantic stopper reduces operational tokens by 38% relative to max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81), whereas the full quality-gated variant is counter-productive because its per-round judging dominates cost. An oracle that selects the best round attains +0.115 Information Score over every practical policy (p ~ 4e-11), reframing the problem from "when to stop" (easy) to "which round is best" (open).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes semantic early-stopping for multi-agent LLM loops (Writer-Critic) using cosine distance of embeddings and quality improvement, replacing fixed iteration caps. It provides theoretical guarantees, a judge-efficient evaluation protocol, and empirical results on HotpotQA showing 38% token reduction without quality loss, while identifying "which round is best" as the open problem.
AI.motivation: Fixed iteration caps for multi-agent LLM loops (e.g., Writer-Critic) are a syntactic kill-switch that wastes tokens on easy inputs and truncates hard ones, since the termination is blind to whether the answer is still improving.
AI.method: Semantic early-stopping: halt when consecutive draft embeddings stop changing (cosine distance with patience window) and quality stops improving. Theoretical proof of deterministic termination. Judge-efficient evaluation: generate full trajectory once, replay stopping policies, cache LLM-judge calls. Empirical study on HotpotQA.
AI.result: Judge-free semantic stopper reduces operational tokens by 38% vs. max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81). Full quality-gated variant is counter-productive due to judging cost. Oracle that selects best round attains +0.115 IS over any practical policy.
AI.conclusion: Semantic early-stopping is viable and token-efficient, but the true challenge is predicting which round is best (open problem) rather than when to stop (solved).

title: How to evaluate clustering with ground truth?
comment: Preprint of a book chapter to appear: P. Fränti, "How to evaluate clustering with ground truth?", In Center-based clustering, Springer Nature, 2026
summary: External indexes can be used for cluster evaluation when ground truth is available. We review the most common external validity indexes focusing on set-matching-based measures. We recommend centroid index (CI), because it is an intuitive cluster-level measure with an explainable result. If we need a more fine-tuned, point-level measure, there are more choices. Pair-set index (PSI) provides a normalized score which is not biased by cluster sizes. If all points should matter equally, then clustering accuracy (ACC) or any other set-matching measure is suitable.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews external validity indexes for cluster evaluation, focusing on set-matching-based measures, and recommends centroid index (CI) as an intuitive cluster-level measure, while discussing other options like Pair-set index (PSI) and clustering accuracy (ACC) for different needs.
AI.motivation: To review common external validity indexes for cluster evaluation when ground truth is available, focusing on set-matching-based measures, and to provide recommendations for different evaluation needs.
AI.method: The paper reviews external cluster validity indexes, specifically set-matching-based measures, and compares their properties such as interpretability, bias, and granularity (cluster-level vs. point-level).
AI.result: Centroid index (CI) is recommended as an intuitive cluster-level measure with explainable results; Pair-set index (PSI) provides a normalized score unbiased by cluster sizes; clustering accuracy (ACC) or other set-matching measures are suitable when all points should matter equally.
AI.conclusion: Different external validity indexes serve different purposes: CI for cluster-level interpretability, PSI for unbiased point-level scoring, and ACC for equal point importance.

title: Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for Large Language Model Agents
summary: For LLM agents in multi-step interactive environments, a key challenge is to make effective use of accumulated interaction experience. Existing work has typically separated two uses of such experience: keeping it outside the model as natural-language rules for later prompting, or using trajectories and feedback to update the model parameters. The former is easy to interpret but can fall out of sync with the evolving policy; the latter improves the policy more broadly but provides only limited correction for local mistakes in sparse-reward settings. We present Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for LLM Agents (JERP), which updates a long-term experiential-rule pool and the policy from the same interaction trajectories. At decision time, JERP retrieves task-relevant rules and conditions the agent on them together with the interaction history. After each episode, it uses the collected trajectories both to optimize the policy and to revise the rule pool by comparing current rollouts with reference successful trajectories. This coupling keeps the rule pool aligned with the evolving policy while allowing stable and effective behaviors to be gradually absorbed into the model itself. Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop show that JERP yields consistent gains in decision performance for complex interactive tasks.

AI.tldr: JERP jointly updates an experiential rule pool and LLM agent policy from the same interaction trajectories, keeping rules aligned with the evolving policy while enabling stable behaviors to be absorbed into the model, achieving consistent gains on AlfWorld and WebShop.
AI.motivation: Existing work separates experience into either external natural-language rules (interpretable but can fall out of sync) or parameter updates (broader improvement but limited local correction in sparse-reward settings). JERP aims to combine both approaches for better decision performance in multi-step interactive environments.
AI.method: JERP maintains a long-term experiential-rule pool. At decision time, it retrieves task-relevant rules and conditions the agent on them alongside interaction history. After each episode, it uses collected trajectories to both optimize the policy and revise the rule pool by comparing current rollouts with reference successful trajectories.
AI.result: Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent gains in decision performance for complex interactive tasks.
AI.conclusion: Coupling rule pool updates with policy optimization keeps the rule pool aligned with the evolving policy while allowing stable behaviors to be gradually absorbed into the model itself, outperforming approaches that treat experience as purely external rules or solely parameter updates.

title: OpenRCA 2.0: From Outcome Labels to Causal Process Supervision
summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) poses a holistic test of LLM agentic capabilities, such as long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, and tool use. However, existing datasets suffer from a fundamental gap: they label only the root cause, not the propagation path connecting it to the observed symptom, which largely simplifies the task to naive pattern matching. To support rigorous evaluation, we introduce PAVE, a step-wise labeling protocol that leverages known interventions from fault injection to reconstruct causal propagation paths. The mechanism is forward verification: reasoning from cause to effect rather than inferring backward from symptoms. Applying PAVE yields OpenRCA 2.0 (500 instances), the first cross-system RCA benchmark with step-wise causal annotations for LLM agents. Across 11 frontier LLMs, recovering the exact root-cause set succeeds in only 20.7% of cases on average. To locate where this difficulty lies, we relax the criterion and find what we call the ungrounded diagnosis: agents identify at least one correct root-cause service in 76.0% of cases, but ground that service in a verified causal propagation path to the observed symptom in only 61.5%. Outcome-only evaluation hides this failure mode; step-wise causal ground truth is the missing piece for trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents.

AI.tldr: PAVE introduces a step-wise causal annotation protocol for RCA benchmarks, yielding OpenRCA 2.0 (500 instances). Evaluation of 11 LLMs reveals that while agents identify correct root-cause services in 76.0% of cases, they ground them in verified causal propagation paths only 61.5% of the time, exposing an "ungrounded diagnosis" failure mode hidden by outcome-only evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing RCA datasets label only the root cause, not the causal propagation path from symptom to root cause, simplifying the task to pattern matching and preventing rigorous evaluation of LLM agentic capabilities (long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, tool use).
AI.method: PAVE (a step-wise labeling protocol) leverages known interventions from fault injection to reconstruct causal propagation paths via forward verification (reasoning from cause to effect). Applied to create OpenRCA 2.0, the first cross-system RCA benchmark with step-wise causal annotations.
AI.result: Across 11 frontier LLMs, exact root-cause set recovery succeeds in only 20.7% of cases. Agents identify at least one correct root-cause service in 76.0% of cases but ground it in a verified causal propagation path in only 61.5%, revealing "ungrounded diagnosis."
AI.conclusion: Outcome-only evaluation hides the ungrounded diagnosis failure mode; step-wise causal ground truth is essential for trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents.

title: TOPS: First-Principles Visual Token Pruning via Constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets for Efficient MLLM Inference
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, but their efficiency is limited by the large number of visual tokens, which introduces substantial computational overhead. Visual token pruning offers a natural solution, yet existing methods are imperfect: attention-based criteria tend to retain redundant tokens, while diversity-based criteria are often agnostic to user instructions. Even methods that combine multiple criteria still lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic objective of token pruning. In this paper, we revisit visual token pruning from a first-principles perspective and formulate it as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets. Through a top-down information-theoretic analysis, we identify three fundamental principles for effective token selection: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. Based on these principles, we propose TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic pruning module that can be applied to various MLLMs. Extensive experiments on 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks demonstrate that TOPS outperforms prior methods under diverse pruning settings. Notably, on LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS removes 77.8% of visual tokens while preserving 100.0% and 100.6% performance on its 7B and 13B models, respectively, suggesting that pruning redundant visual tokens can sometimes mitigate hallucination and inspire future lightweight MLLM design.

AI.tldr: TOPS formulates visual token pruning in MLLMs as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets via three principles (Task Relevance, Information Coverage, Semantic Diversity), achieving 77.8% token removal while preserving or slightly improving performance across 7 backbones and 14 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: MLLMs suffer from computational overhead due to excessive visual tokens. Existing pruning methods are imperfect: attention-based criteria retain redundant tokens, diversity-based criteria ignore user instructions, and combined approaches lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic pruning objective.
AI.method: The paper derives three fundamental pruning principles (Task Relevance, Information Coverage, Semantic Diversity) via information-theoretic analysis, and proposes TOPS—a training-free, model-agnostic pruning module that constructs Token Optimal Preservation Sets based on these principles.
AI.result: TOPS outperforms prior methods across 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks. On LLaVA-NeXT, removing 77.8% of visual tokens preserves 100.0% (7B) and 100.6% (13B) performance, showing pruning can sometimes mitigate hallucination.
AI.conclusion: Pruning redundant visual tokens can maintain or even improve MLLM performance while reducing computational cost, and TOPS provides a principled, training-free solution applicable to various MLLMs.

title: A Process Harness for Uplifting Legacy Workflows to Agentic BPM: Design and Realization in CUGA FLO
summary: We introduce the process harness, a new mechanism for uplifting legacy workflows into Agentic Business Process Management (Agentic BPM) without replacing the underlying workflow engine. A process harness places a policy-governed agentic layer around a deterministic workflow engine, intercepting designated control points to contribute reasoning, adaptation, and oversight while the engine retains structural authority over the process. To define the process harness rigorously, we develop the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model, specifying both its data schema and its execution semantics. TDF decomposes LLM reasoning across three policy-governed agent types: a TaskAgent for knowledge-intensive task execution, a DecisionAgent for per-case gateway routing, and a FlowAgent that governs runtime flow adaptation through a principled hook mechanism. Each agent reasons within an explicit policy drawn from the process FRAME, the aggregate policy set governing all LLM calls in the system. We then present CUGA FLO as the design and implementation realization of the TDF model, and demonstrate it on a loan approval workflow that exercises all three agent types and hook-driven regulatory override. The process harness uniquely reconciles imperative requirements, realized through deterministic workflow execution that enforces structural compliance, with normative requirements, realized through policy-framed agentic autonomy invoked at designated control points wherever the process demands it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the process harness, a mechanism that wraps legacy workflows with a policy-governed agentic layer (TaskAgent, DecisionAgent, FlowAgent) to enable Agentic BPM without replacing the underlying deterministic workflow engine, formalized via the TDF model and implemented as CUGA FLO.
AI.motivation: To uplift legacy deterministic workflows into Agentic BPM without replacing the existing workflow engine, reconciling imperative structural compliance with normative agentic autonomy.
AI.method: The authors develop the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model with data schema and execution semantics, defining three policy-governed agent types (TaskAgent, DecisionAgent, FlowAgent) that operate via a hook mechanism within a process harness, guided by the process FRAME policy set. They implement this as CUGA FLO.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a loan approval workflow that exercises all three agent types and hook-driven regulatory override, showing that the process harness enables policy-framed agentic reasoning at designated control points while the deterministic engine retains structural authority.
AI.conclusion: The process harness uniquely reconciles imperative requirements (deterministic structural compliance) with normative requirements (policy-framed agentic autonomy), enabling non-disruptive adoption of Agentic BPM in legacy systems.

title: Vulnerability of Natural Language Classifiers to Evolutionary Generated Adversarial Text
summary: Deep learning models have achieved impressive performance across various fields but remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs, particularly in NLP, where such attacks can have significant real-world consequences. Adversarial attacks often involve small, semantically similar token replacements to fool NLP models, and recent methods have become more precise by targeting specific vulnerable words, often by exploiting some level of access to the model's internal structure. This paper proposes GAversary, a hybrid Genetic Algorithm (GA) to generate adversarial attacks on natural language models. The GA is able to treat the target model as a black box, requiring only the logit value output by the model to guide the search. GAversary differs from GAs previously proposed for this problem by using GloVe embeddings to propose word replacements (the mutation operator) to improve the semantic similarity of the adversarial examples. GAversary is applied to several benchmark data sets and well-known target models. GAversary is able to substantially reduce the target model's accuracy on test data compared to the BAE and A2T attacks compared against (in the best case, reducing a 76.8% accuracy to 5.8%, compared to BAE's 27.6%). The trade-off is that GAversary perturbs just under twice as many words as the other two methods, with a slightly lower semantic similarity to the original text and around a 5% increase in run-time.

AI.tldr: GAversary is a hybrid Genetic Algorithm that generates black-box adversarial attacks on NLP models using GloVe embeddings for semantically similar word replacements, achieving substantial accuracy reductions (e.g., 76.8% to 5.8%) at the cost of more perturbed words and slightly lower similarity.
AI.motivation: NLP models are vulnerable to adversarial inputs with real-world consequences; existing attack methods require model access or lack precision, motivating a black-box approach that generates semantically similar adversarial examples.
AI.method: A hybrid Genetic Algorithm (GA) is proposed that treats the target model as a black box, using only logit outputs to guide the search. It employs GloVe embeddings as the mutation operator to propose semantically similar word replacements.
AI.result: GAversary substantially reduces target model accuracy compared to BAE and A2T baselines (best case: 76.8% to 5.8% vs. BAE's 27.6%), but perturbs nearly twice as many words with slightly lower semantic similarity and ~5% longer runtime.
AI.conclusion: GAversary is an effective black-box adversarial attack for NLP that trades higher perturbation rate and runtime for significantly greater accuracy reduction and semantic similarity preservation via GloVe-enhanced genetic search.

title: Ask, Don't Judge: Binary Questions for Interpretable LLM Evaluation and Self-Improvement
comment: Acceepted to the Second Workshop on Compositional Learning at ICML 2026, Seoul, South Korea
summary: Evaluating LLM outputs remains a major bottleneck in NLP: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics correlate poorly with human judgments on open-ended generation, and holistic LLM judges often produce opaque scores that are hard to debug. We propose BINEVAL, a framework that decomposes evaluation criteria into atomic binary questions and aggregates the resulting verdicts into interpretable, multi-dimensional scores. Given a task prompt, a meta-prompt generates fine-grained evaluation questions, and an LLM answers them independently for each output, yielding transparent question-level feedback together with calibrated overall scores. This decomposition makes evaluation easier to inspect, easier to diagnose, and directly usable for prompt improvement. Across SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, BINEVAL matches or outperforms strong baselines including UniEval and G-Eval, with especially strong results on factual consistency benchmarks such as QAGS. Beyond competitive correlation with human judgments, BINEVAL better matches human score distributions and avoids the ceiling effects common in prior LLM judges, leading to better discrimination between borderline and clearly flawed outputs. We further show that the same question-level feedback supports iterative prompt optimization, improving evaluator prompts on summarization and generation prompts on IFBench under both self-update and cross-model update settings. Overall, BINEVAL provides a task-agnostic, training-free, and interpretable evaluation framework that combines strong empirical performance with practical diagnostic and optimization value.

AI.tldr: BINEVAL decomposes evaluation criteria into atomic binary questions answered by an LLM, producing interpretable multi-dimensional scores that match or outperform existing methods like UniEval and G-Eval on SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, while also supporting iterative prompt optimization.
AI.motivation: Evaluating LLM outputs is a major bottleneck: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics correlate poorly with human judgments on open-ended generation, and holistic LLM judges produce opaque scores that are hard to debug.
AI.method: BINEVAL decomposes evaluation criteria into atomic binary questions via a meta-prompt, then an LLM answers each question independently per output, yielding transparent question-level feedback and calibrated aggregated scores.
AI.result: Matches or outperforms UniEval and G-Eval on SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS; strong on factual consistency (QAGS); better matches human score distributions and avoids ceiling effects; supports iterative prompt optimization under self-update and cross-model settings.
AI.conclusion: BINEVAL is a task-agnostic, training-free, interpretable evaluation framework combining strong empirical performance with practical diagnostic and optimization value.

title: EO-WM: A Physically Informed World Model for Probabilistic Earth Observation Forecasting
summary: Earth Observation (EO) forecasting aims to predict future Earth surface dynamics from satellite observations under changing meteorological conditions. In this paper, we view this task as a partially observed, weather-driven world modeling problem, in which weather acts as a conditioning signal, while forecasting remains uncertain due to sparse observations and unobserved land-surface states. However, existing methods do not fully capture this setting: deterministic models collapse uncertainty into a single future prediction, while diffusion-based methods typically treat weather variables as undifferentiated conditioning signals, and existing benchmarks focus mainly on reconstruction accuracy rather than whether forecasts respond correctly to changed weather forcing.We introduce EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer for multispectral EO forecasting. EO-WM incorporates a physically informed conditioning framework that represents meteorological forcing through a climatological baseline, weather anomalies, and cumulative physical stress signals. Specifically, it separates baseline and anomaly through distinct conditioning pathways, and accumulates anomalous forcing over time to capture sustained heat and drought stress. To evaluate weather-response behavior beyond standard metrics, we introduce two diagnostic benchmarks: an Extreme Summer Benchmark for severity-aware prediction of vegetation degradation under extreme weather, and a Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark for testing response fidelity under changed weather forcing. Experiments show that EO-WM reduces the error in predicted Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) decline amplitude by a relative 5.63% and improves directional hit rate by a relative 7.80%, while remaining competitive on standard pixel-level metrics. The benchmarks and model will be made open-source at https://github.com/Luo-Z13/EO-WM.

AI.tldr: EO-WM is a video diffusion transformer for Earth Observation forecasting that uses a physically informed conditioning framework separating climatological baselines from weather anomalies and cumulative stress signals. It introduces two diagnostic benchmarks (Extreme Summer and Seasonal Matched-Pair) to evaluate weather-response behavior, achieving improvements in NDVI decline amplitude error (-5.63%) and directional hit rate (+7.80%).
AI.motivation: Existing EO forecasting methods fail to capture the partially observed, weather-driven world modeling nature of the task: deterministic models collapse uncertainty, diffusion methods treat weather as undifferentiated conditioning, and benchmarks focus on reconstruction accuracy rather than correct response to changed weather forcing.
AI.method: EO-WM is a video diffusion transformer with a physically informed conditioning framework that (1) separates climatological baseline and weather anomalies through distinct conditioning pathways, and (2) accumulates anomalous forcing over time to capture sustained heat and drought stress. Two diagnostic benchmarks are proposed: Extreme Summer (severity-aware prediction of vegetation degradation) and Seasonal Matched-Pair (response fidelity under changed weather).
AI.result: EO-WM reduces NDVI decline amplitude error by 5.63% and improves directional hit rate by 7.80% relative to baselines, while remaining competitive on standard pixel-level metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed physically informed conditioning and diagnostic benchmarks better capture weather-response behavior in EO forecasting, addressing limitations of existing methods and evaluation protocols.

title: Simulation-based inference for rapid Bayesian parameter estimation in epidemiological models: a comparison with MCMC
summary: Mechanistic epidemiological models are widely used to support infectious disease forecasting and public-health decision making. Bayesian calibration of such models is commonly performed using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which can become computationally expensive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and repeated near-real-time analyses. Here, we investigate simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation as a scalable alternative for Bayesian calibration of a mechanistic SECIR epidemiological model using COVID-19 intensive care unit (ICU) occupancy data from Germany during 2020. We compared SBI and MCMC across multiple epidemic phases using both 31-day inference windows and a substantially more challenging 201-day reconstruction problem involving multiple transmission change points. Posterior agreement was evaluated quantitatively using Wasserstein distances and Kullback-Leibler divergences together with posterior predictive checks. Across the 31-day windows, SBI recovered posterior distributions in strong agreement with MCMC while accurately reproducing observed ICU trajectories. In the 201-day setting, SBI preserved the dominant posterior structure despite increased uncertainty. SBI, by combining CPU and GPU resources, substantially reduced computational runtime compared with MCMC, which was restricted to running on CPUs. Whereas MCMC required approximately 1000 seconds for the 31-day inference problems, SBI achieved comparable posterior and predictive performance in approximately 60-70 seconds on a single GPU. For the 201-day inference problem, SBI required an average of 157 seconds, while the MCMC runs took over 19,000 seconds. Our results demonstrate that SBI provides a rapid and computationally efficient framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, supporting repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation can serve as a fast and computationally efficient alternative to MCMC for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, achieving comparable posterior accuracy while reducing runtime from ~1000s to ~60-70s (31-day windows) and from ~19,000s to ~157s (201-day windows) using COVID-19 ICU data from Germany.
AI.motivation: Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models using MCMC is computationally expensive, especially for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and repeated near-real-time analyses, motivating the need for a scalable alternative.
AI.method: The authors compared simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation against MCMC for calibrating a mechanistic SECIR model, using COVID-19 ICU occupancy data from Germany across multiple epidemic phases with both 31-day and 201-day inference windows. Posterior agreement was evaluated using Wasserstein distances, KL divergences, and posterior predictive checks.
AI.result: SBI recovered posterior distributions in strong agreement with MCMC while accurately reproducing observed ICU trajectories. SBI reduced runtime from ~1000s (MCMC) to ~60-70s (SBI) for 31-day windows, and from ~19,000s (MCMC) to ~157s (SBI) for the 201-day inference problem.
AI.conclusion: SBI provides a rapid and computationally efficient framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, supporting repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis.

title: Prompt Injection in Automated Résumé Screening with Large Language Models: Single and Multi-Injection Settings
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to screen and rank job applicants, creating incentives for candidates to strategically manipulate algorithmic hiring systems. We study prompt injection in automated résumé screening, defined as subtle self-promotional text that introduces no new qualifications but is designed to influence LLM evaluations. Using controlled experiments, we show that prompt injection reliably improves applicant rankings when résumé quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject. However, its effectiveness rapidly diminishes as more candidates inject, collapsing when manipulation becomes widespread. When candidate quality is heterogeneous, prompt injection is less effective on average, but can occasionally allow lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones, raising fairness concerns. Overall, LLM-based screening is most vulnerable when manipulation is rare and candidate quality differences are small. Code and resources are publicly available at: https://github.com/preetb1199/Prompt_Injection_ACL26

AI.tldr: This paper studies prompt injection in LLM-based résumé screening, finding it can improve applicant rankings when manipulation is rare and candidate quality is homogeneous, but becomes ineffective when widespread or when quality differences are large.
AI.motivation: To understand how strategic prompt injection (subtle self-promotional text) can manipulate LLM-based automated hiring systems, and to assess the fairness and robustness of such systems under adversarial conditions.
AI.method: Controlled experiments varying manipulation prevalence (few vs. many injectors) and candidate quality (homogeneous vs. heterogeneous) to measure the impact of prompt injection on LLM-based résumé ranking.
AI.result: Prompt injection reliably boosts rankings when résumé quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject, but collapses when manipulation is widespread. Under heterogeneous quality, injection is less effective on average but can cause lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based screening is most vulnerable when manipulation is rare and candidate quality differences are minimal, posing fairness concerns in such scenarios.

title: When Does Combining Language Models Help? A Co-Failure Ceiling on Routing, Voting, and Mixture-of-Agents Across 67 Frontier Models
summary:
Multi-model LLM systems such as routing, voting, cascades, fusion, and mixture-of-agents are used to beat single-model accuracy. We show that their gain is capped by a quantity the field rarely reports. For any policy whose output is one member model answer, accuracy cannot exceed one minus beta, where beta is the rate at which every model is wrong on the same query. In contrast, the usual diagnostic, average pairwise error correlation rho, cannot identify beta: error laws with identical marginals and pairwise correlations can have different all-wrong rates. A Clopper-Pearson bound on beta gives a finite-sample certificate on the largest gain any router, vote, or cascade could deliver before training a router.
  Across 67 models from 21 providers, a tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor model still underprices the all-wrong tail: on open-ended mathematics, observed beta is 0.052 versus 0.023 under the full 67-model Gaussian copula, about 2.5 times underpricing, with 90 percent CI 1.7 to 3.4 and k equals 17. The effect recurs on execution-graded code, where beta is 0.079. Re-asking the same GPQA-Diamond questions in free-response rather than multiple-choice form reopens the tail, with beta 0.127 and a five-judge panel with kappa 0.73 to 0.92, locating co-failure in answer format rather than subject. At matched quality, low-rho heterogeneous ensembles beat high-rho Self-MoA, but on checkable tasks in our pool, combining models rarely beats the single best model without a strong query-level routing signal. Gains come from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models.

AI.tldr: Multi-model LLM systems have accuracy capped by the "all-wrong rate" β (rate where every model fails on the same query), computed as 1-β. Standard metric ρ (pairwise error correlation) cannot identify β. Empirical results across 67 models show β is systematically underpredicted by Gaussian copula models (e.g., 0.052 observed vs 0.023 predicted on math). Gains from combining models come from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to identify and measure the fundamental upper bound on accuracy improvements from multi-model LLM systems (routing, voting, cascades, fusion, MoA), showing that the field's usual diagnostic (pairwise error correlation ρ) is insufficient and that the "all-wrong rate" β is the true limiting factor.
AI.method: The authors derive a theoretical bound: for any policy outputting one member model answer, accuracy ≤ 1-β where β is the rate every model is wrong. They use Clopper-Pearson for finite-sample certificates. Empirically, they evaluate 67 models from 21 providers on open-ended math and execution-graded code, using tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor models and Gaussian copulas to compare predicted vs observed β.
AI.result: Observed β (0.052 on math, 0.079 on code) is ~2.5× higher than Gaussian copula predictions (0.023 on math). GPQA-Diamond free-response yields β=0.127. Low-ρ heterogeneous ensembles beat high-ρ Self-MoA at matched quality. Combining models rarely beats the single best model without strong query-level routing.
AI.conclusion: Multi-model gains are fundamentally capped by the all-wrong rate β, not pairwise error correlation ρ. Gains come from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models. The field should report β as a diagnostic for ensemble potential.

title: Language-Based Digital Twins for Elderly Cognitive Assistance
comment: Accepted and published in the Proceedings of the ACM International Conference on PErvasive Technologies Related to Assistive Environments (PETRA 2026). The final published version is available through the ACM Digital Library
summary: Digital twins have emerged as a promising paradigm for personalized healthcare, enabling modeling of individual behavior and health trajectories. In cognitive health, early detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) remains challenging, where language and conversational patterns serve as non-invasive biomarkers. In this work, we propose a language-based digital twin framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to mimic the conversational behavior of elderly individuals by incorporating stylometric cues and contextual metadata. To evaluate fidelity and cognitive consistency, we introduce a multi-head conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) that jointly measures reconstruction quality and predicts cognitive scores. Experiments on the I-CONECT dataset show that the digital twin preserves identity-specific characteristics and achieves reconstruction and MoCA prediction errors comparable to real data, while outperforming baseline GPT-generated responses. These results highlight the potential of language-based digital twins as a scalable and non-invasive approach for personalized and continuous cognitive health monitoring.

AI.tldr: A language-based digital twin framework using LLMs with stylometric cues and contextual metadata to mimic elderly conversational behavior for MCI detection, evaluated via a multi-head cVAE that measures reconstruction quality and cognitive scores.
AI.motivation: Early detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) remains challenging; language and conversational patterns serve as non-invasive biomarkers but existing approaches lack personalized modeling of individual behavior and health trajectories.
AI.method: 1) A language-based digital twin framework using LLMs that incorporates stylometric cues and contextual metadata to mimic elderly conversational behavior. 2) A multi-head conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) jointly measuring reconstruction quality and predicting cognitive scores (MoCA).
AI.result: On the I-CONECT dataset, the digital twin preserves identity-specific characteristics, achieves reconstruction and MoCA prediction errors comparable to real data, and outperforms baseline GPT-generated responses.
AI.conclusion: Language-based digital twins are a scalable and non-invasive approach for personalized and continuous cognitive health monitoring.
